fits: Video calls with grandparents and family far away, with a parent holding the phone.
Music, lullabies and scripture stories played aloud while you hold them.
A parent's phone camera, to keep the memories.
bless: Let them see grandma's face and hear her voice every week.
Sing the same lullaby every night; it becomes home to them.
ages.label: Babies & Toddlers
rules: No screen time except video chat with family (American Academy of Pediatrics).
No screens in the room where they sleep.
Never a screen to stop crying; hold them instead.
watch: A baby who stops looking up at faces, or whose words come late, when screens are on a lot.
Background television: it cuts the number of words a baby hears from you.
ages.growing: Attachment, trust, first words and walking. A baby learns language from a face that answers back, not from a screen; this is the age when the brain wires itself fastest around real people.

fits: Picture books and scripture stories on a screen, read together, the way you would read a book.
Children's music and hymns.
Drawing and building apps, for short spells, beside you.
bless: Record a message or a song for someone who is sick or far away.
Make a card on the tablet and print it for a neighbor.
ages.label: Early Years
rules: About an hour a day at most, of good content, watched with a parent (American Academy of Pediatrics); the WHO says an hour or less for this age too.
No screens at meals, in the car for short trips, or in the hour before bed.
You choose the content; autoplay is off; no 'kids' video feeds unwatched.
watch: Tantrums when the screen goes off, and asking for it first thing in the morning.
Fast, flashing cartoons; they train a short attention span.
Advertisements aimed at them; explain what an ad is.
ages.growing: Imagination, language, self-control, and the first sense of right and wrong. They copy everything, cannot yet tell a story from an advertisement, and feel a sudden stop like a loss.

fits: Learning apps and reading apps, with the settings you chose.
Family video calls, family movie night, uplifting shows chosen together.
Simple creation: drawing, music, photos of family, a first typed story.
bless: Video-call an older relative and ask them a family-history question; record the answer.
Type a thank-you note to a teacher or a church leader.
ages.label: Early Elementary
rules: Consistent daily limits, written down as a family media plan; screens live in family rooms, never bedrooms.
No personal smartphone, no social media, no online games with strangers' chat.
Filters on every device, and a parent who can see the history.
watch: Fear from something they saw; ask 'did you see anything that scared you?' often.
Sneaking screens, or lying about time.
Comparing themselves with children on a screen.
ages.growing: Reading, friendship, fairness, and a conscience that can be taught. They believe what they see. They want to belong, and they still tell you everything if you make it safe to.

fits: Homework and learning online in a family room, with filters and history visible.
Creating: coding, music, film-making, photography, with the results shared inside the family.
A watch or basic phone that calls and texts, only if the family truly needs it; a smartphone can wait.
bless: Teach a younger sibling something on the tablet.
Help a grandparent with their phone; that is service too.
Make a family video for a birthday or a farewell.
ages.label: Late Elementary
rules: No social media (the law sets 13 as the floor for most apps).
No devices in bedrooms overnight; they charge in the kitchen.
A family rule that a secret online is never kept from parents, and that closing a bad page and telling is always the right move, never punished.
watch: Withdrawal, secrecy, a screen that is always turned away.
Sleep loss, and mood that tracks the screen.
Anyone online who wants to move the talk to a private app.
ages.growing: Competence, rules and fairness, and friends who start to matter as much as family. Curiosity is strong and the brakes are not built yet. Many children first meet pornography by accident around the end of this stage, so the talk comes before the device.

fits: A first phone with a written family agreement, filters, and a parent who knows every account and password.
Tools to create and serve: editing, design, coding, music, a family history project.
Scripture and hymn apps, and talks they choose to listen to.
bless: Share a kindness, a scripture or a testimony online on purpose, not by accident.
Organize a service project with friends through the group chat.
Record grandparents' stories and put them on the family timeline.
ages.label: Early Adolescence
rules: Delay social media as long as you can (13 is the legal floor, and the U.S. Surgeon General warns it is not proof of safety); if it is used, accounts are private, parents follow, notifications are off, and there is a daily limit.
Phones out of bedrooms at night and off the table at meals.
Talk plainly about pornography, sextortion, bullying and AI 'companions' before they meet them; agree what they will do when they do.
watch: Three hours a day or more on social media doubles the risk of anxiety and depression symptoms (U.S. Surgeon General, 2023).
A sudden new 'friend' who sends gifts or asks for pictures.
Comparing their body or their life to a feed.
ages.growing: Identity, puberty, the pull of friends, and a hunger for approval that social media is built to exploit. The part of the brain that weighs consequences is still growing until the mid-twenties. Faith begins to become their own here.

fits: Their own limits, written by them and reviewed with you.
AI, design, code and media as tools for real work, school and service.
Teaching the younger ones what they have learned.
bless: Lead a family history project; build the family's timeline.
Create something that lifts: music, a short film, a page that helps someone.
Use the tools to reach, to teach and to serve.
ages.label: Teen
rules: Phones away at meals and when people are present, and out of the bedroom at night.
A weekly time away from screens, together as a family.
Learn to tell truth from propaganda: check who made it, who paid for it, and what it wants you to feel.
watch: Driving with a phone in hand.
Gambling built into games and apps.
Letting an AI do the thinking, the writing, or the feeling.
ages.growing: Abstract thinking, the need to be their own person, and the first practice at governing themselves: driving, work, money, choices about what to watch and who to follow. Risk still feels smaller than it is.

fits: Every tool their schooling, work and service need, used on purpose.
Their own standards, kept because they chose them.
Mentoring younger brothers, sisters and cousins.
bless: Lead the family history and temple work, or the family's record keeping.
Use AI, design, code and media for real service.
Reach, teach and gather: use the tools the way the Lord's work uses them.
ages.label: Young Adult
rules: Choose your own limits, write them down, and keep them.
Guard sleep, real friendships and time with God from the feed.
Keep the standards of your faith as your own.
watch: Hours lost to endless feeds and games.
Online debt, gambling and scams.
An AI that does the work you were meant to learn.
ages.growing: Governing themselves fully: college, missions and service, work, marriage. The rules are now theirs; a parent becomes a counselor they come back to.

bad: Burning what belongs to other people.
Using it carelessly so it spreads.
Hurting animals or land with it on purpose.
items.why: Fire is the first light people could hold. It gathered families around it at night - the first bedtime circle. Cooked food helped people grow strong and think clearly, ready one day to hear and understand the word of God.

ages.0-2: Never within reach. 'Hot' is one of the first words worth teaching.
ages.16+: Teach the younger ones fire safety; carry the responsibility.
ages.3-5: Watch a campfire from a parent's arms; learn that fire is a helper only when a grown-up holds it.
ages.6-9: Help gather wood and feed a campfire with a grown-up right beside them.
ages.10-12: Light a candle or a stove with permission, and learn how to put a fire out.
ages.13-15: Build, tend and fully put out a campfire; cook a meal on it.

good: Cooking food so it is safe and good to eat.
Keeping a family warm and together on a cold night.
Light to read and talk by after the sun goes down.
harm: Burns and house fires: fire does not know a child from a log.
A fascination with flames that grows if it is a secret.
kids: Only grown-ups light it.
Never leave a fire alone.
Fire is for warming and cooking, never for showing off.
items.name: Fire
items.talk: Fire can cook our dinner or burn our house. What makes the difference?
items.what: People learned to keep a fire and to make one. Warmth, light in the dark, cooked food, and a safe place to gather.
avoid: Matches, lighters and candles left where small hands reach.
Fireworks in a child's hands.
Playing near a stove, a campfire or a heater.
bless: Cook a meal for a family that needs one.
A campfire family night, with stories of the pioneers who cooked over one every night.
Bring warmth to someone: soup, a blanket, a lit porch.
dangers: A fire nobody watches grows fast.
Smoke in a closed room can hurt you.
A wildfire can take homes in an hour.

learned.note: The story never changes: fire blesses the careful and hurts the careless. That is the pattern every later technology follows.

stages.0-2: Babies and toddlers should not touch or play with fire. They move fast, reach for bright things and do not yet understand "hot." Keep them behind gates and screens, away from fireplaces, wood stoves, fire pits and hot drinks, and remember that the glass front of a gas fireplace can stay hot for up to an hour after it is turned off.
stages.3-5: Little children can watch a candle or campfire from a lap or behind a line you draw on the ground. Teach them that fire is a tool for grown-ups, not a toy, and that if they find matches or a lighter they should tell a grown-up and not touch them. Children this age are naturally curious, so answer their questions calmly instead of scaring them.
stages.6-8: Early elementary children can help with fire in small ways while you watch, such as roasting a marshmallow from outside a three-foot "circle of safety." They can also practice your family's fire escape plan and learn to stop, drop and roll. They are learning rules quickly, but they still need you right there, because flame burns from fire play become more common at this age.
stages.9-11: Older children can learn to strike a match or light a candle with a parent beside them, and to put a fire out with water. When they learn the right way in the open, fire is less of a mystery, and they are less likely to try it in secret. If a child keeps setting fires or won't stop playing with lighters, your local fire department can help.
stages.12-14: Young teens can cook on the stove and help build and put out a campfire, with an adult nearby. They are building judgment but still take risks, so keep clear rules: no gasoline or other flammable liquids on a fire, and leave fireworks to the professionals.
stages.15-17: Teens can cook alone and look after a campfire or fireplace, as long as they show they can do it safely and know what to do in an emergency. Burn injuries rise again in the mid-teens, so talk openly about peer dares, fireworks and fuels while trusting them with real responsibility.
stages.18+: Young adults should be able to keep a home and a camp safe on their own. That means working smoke alarms, a fire extinguisher, a practiced escape plan and safe cooking habits. Now they are the ones who teach and protect younger children.

studies.finding: The American Academy of Pediatrics advises putting smoke alarms outside bedrooms and on every floor, keeping fire extinguishers where fires are most likely, never leaving cooking on the stove unattended, practicing family fire drills, and teaching children to stop, drop and roll if their clothes catch fire.
studies.source: American Academy of Pediatrics, HealthyChildren.org – Burn Treatment & Prevention Tips for Families

studies.finding: Children around backyard fire pits and campfires can be burned by flames, by hot surfaces or by falling into hot ashes. Coals can stay hot for more than 24 hours. Pediatricians advise always watching children around fires and drawing a 'circle of safety' at least 3 feet around a fire that children do not cross.
studies.source: AAP News – Follow safety measures around outdoor fires to prevent injury

studies.finding: Curiosity about fire is normal in children. The U.S. Fire Administration advises teaching that fire is a tool, not a toy, keeping matches and lighters away from children, supervising them, practicing a home fire escape plan, and asking the local fire department for help if a child seems likely to experiment with fire.
studies.source: U.S. Fire Administration (FEMA) – Youth Firesetting

studies.finding: The World Health Organization says many burns happen at home and that children are especially at risk of scalds. It estimated about 35,600 deaths from fire, heat and hot substances among children under 15 worldwide in 2023, and it recommends tested home safety measures such as working smoke alarms, safer water temperatures and safeguards for young children.
studies.source: World Health Organization – Burns fact sheet

studies.finding: A 2025 review of studies found consistent evidence worldwide that breathing wildfire smoke is linked to worse breathing health in children. Research on other effects, such as on physical activity and school, is still early, and the authors call for more long-term study.
studies.source: Syed et al., Paediatric and Perinatal Epidemiology (systematic review)

experts.say: Young children are especially at risk of burns from glass-fronted gas fireplaces, whose glass can stay hot for up to an hour after the fire is off. There is good news, too: new U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission standards require new gas fireplaces to be sold with a safety barrier and information about burn risks.
experts.who: Michael A. Gittelman, MD, FAAP, pediatric emergency physician
experts.source: American Academy of Pediatrics, AAP Voices blog

experts.say: As wildfires grow, smoke is becoming a bigger health threat, especially for young people and children with asthma or other breathing illnesses.
experts.who: Amanda Millstein, MD, FAAP, pediatrician in Northern California
experts.source: American Academy of Pediatrics, AAP Voices blog

experts.say: Cooking and heating with open fires and polluting fuels is still a serious danger in many homes around the world. Household air pollution was linked to over 309,000 deaths of children under 5 in 2021, and women and children carry the heaviest burden, so cleaner, safer ways to cook could save many young lives.
experts.who: World Health Organization
experts.source: WHO – Household air pollution fact sheet

experts.say: The research is still mixed. In a study of children and young people with asthma in Vermont and Upstate New York, asthma control was worse in the very smoky summer of 2023 than in 2022 on two of three measures, but there was no difference when 2023 was compared with 2024.
experts.who: Anna K. Maassel and colleagues, University of Vermont (study in Environmental Health)
experts.source: Drugs.com MedNews (HealthDay) report on the study

future: Cooking safely on a stove, grill or campfire, so they can feed themselves and others well.
Keeping a home safe from fire: testing smoke alarms, using a fire extinguisher, and making and practicing an escape plan.
Building, tending and fully putting out an outdoor fire: clearing the ground, keeping water close, never using gasoline, and making sure the coals are cold.
Reading air-quality and wildfire smoke alerts and knowing how to protect themselves, their children and neighbors who are more at risk.
work: Fire gives warmth and hot meals, so families can open their homes and share food with the hungry, the cold and the lonely, as Jesus fed the multitudes.
Helping families who cook over open fires get cleaner, safer stoves can protect children's lungs and lives, which is a real way to serve the poor around the world.
Knowing fire safety and burn first aid lets us care for the hurt and the sick, and calmly help a neighbor in an emergency.
A warm hearth or campfire is a natural place for families to gather, sing, pray and read the scriptures together, and to remember that Christ is 'the light of the world.'

bad: War chariots were one of its first uses.
Rushing so fast that people get hurt.
items.why: The wheel let people carry more than their arms could hold. Food reached hungry cities, families moved to new lands, and one day the wheel would carry scriptures and missionaries across the world.

ages.0-2: Strollers and wagons pulled by a parent.
ages.16+: Driving: the biggest wheel of all, phone out of reach, every time.
ages.3-5: A tricycle or balance bike, helmet on every time.
ages.6-9: A bike on sidewalks and paths with a grown-up near.
ages.10-12: Rides to a friend's house with agreed routes and times.
ages.13-15: Longer rides; learn the road rules a driver keeps.

good: Carrying food and water to people who need it.
Helping a family travel to be together.
Every machine that helps people work: a mill, a bicycle, a car.
harm: Falls, and roads: the wheel goes faster than a child can judge.
A car treated as a toy or a place to play.
kids: Look both ways.
A cart is for carrying, not for racing.
Help load it for someone who cannot.
items.name: The Wheel
items.talk: What do we carry to other people that they could not get on their own?
items.what: A round thing that rolls. Carts, then chariots, then every machine that turns.
avoid: Riding without a helmet.
Streets without a grown-up until they have earned it.
A driver's seat before the law and the family say so.
bless: Deliver a meal or a note on a bike.
Pull a wagon of groceries for a neighbor.
Learn to fix a bike, then fix someone else's.
dangers: Anything that rolls fast can run someone over.
Machines that turn can catch fingers and clothing.

learned.note: The wheel appears in Mesopotamia on pottery first and carts soon after. Its best use was never the chariot; it was bringing food home.

stages.0-2: Babies and toddlers should ride in a rear-facing car seat, ideally for as long as the seat's height and weight limits allow, because their heads are heavy and their necks are still weak. A car is never a place to leave them alone or let them play, and wheeled walkers and strollers need a grown-up's hand on them.
stages.3-5: Little ones can enjoy tricycles and balance bikes with a helmet, on paths and away from cars, because they cannot yet judge how fast a car is coming. In the car, they ride in a harnessed seat for as long as it fits, and parents can teach them that driveways and parked cars are not for play.
stages.6-8: Children this age can learn to ride a bike with a helmet, on quiet paths with a grown-up nearby, and can start learning simple road rules like stopping, looking, and listening. In the car, most need a booster seat because a seat belt alone does not fit their small bodies yet.
stages.9-11: Children can ride bikes on quiet streets they know well once they have shown they follow the rules, and they should always wear a helmet. Most still need a booster until the seat belt fits, often around 4 feet 9 inches tall, and every child under 13 should ride in the back seat.
stages.12-14: Young teens can ride more on their own, but they still need a helmet every time, and families should think carefully about e-bikes and e-scooters because injuries from them are rising quickly and e-bike injuries tend to be more serious. This is a good time to talk about why rules keep everyone safe, because their sense of risk is still growing.
stages.15-17: Teens learning to drive need plenty of practice with a parent beside them, no phone in their hands, and a slow, step-by-step path toward driving alone, because new drivers are still building judgment. A car is a real responsibility, and it can also be a real blessing: getting to work, church, and serving others.
stages.18+: Young adults can drive and ride on their own, keep their vehicles in good repair, and set a safe example for younger brothers and sisters. They can use wheels to serve, like giving rides to people who have no other way to get to the doctor, to work, or to church.

studies.finding: The American Academy of Pediatrics advises rear-facing car seats from the very first ride home, then a harnessed seat for as long as possible (at least to age 4), then a booster until the belt fits, usually at 4 feet 9 inches and 8 to 12 years old. All children under 13 should ride in the back seat.
studies.source: American Academy of Pediatrics guidance, as summarized by Twiniversity

studies.finding: At one California children's hospital, e-bike and e-scooter injuries in children and teens rose nearly fourfold between 2019 and 2025. E-scooters caused more of the injuries, but e-bike injuries were more serious, and most injuries came from simple falls or losing control.
studies.source: Research presented at the American Academy of Pediatrics 2026 National Conference (EurekAlert! / Healio)

studies.finding: In a study of 285 children hurt on bikes, scooters, and skateboards from 2020 to 2024, only about 1 in 4 wore a helmet, and helmet use went down over those years even as injuries from electric vehicles went up. This was a single-hospital study, so the results may not apply everywhere.
studies.source: Peer-reviewed study, 'Declining helmet use and emerging electric vehicle injuries among pediatric patients presenting wi

studies.finding: A JAMA Surgery study of U.S. emergency room data found that e-bike riders without helmets were almost twice as likely to have head injuries as riders who wore helmets.
studies.source: NPR, reporting on a study in JAMA Surgery

experts.say: Pediatric surgeons warn that e-bike injuries in children are often more severe than injuries from regular bikes, including skull fractures and broken bones, and that rules for young riders have not kept up with how fast e-bikes are spreading.
experts.who: American College of Surgeons, Bulletin
experts.source: Bulletin of the American College of Surgeons, June 2026

experts.say: Better street design, helmet laws, education, and even e-bike riding lessons could help prevent injuries as more people ride.
experts.who: Charles DiMaggio, injury researcher (quoted by NPR)

experts.say: A national study found that e-bike injuries among young people were closer in severity to injuries from gas-powered bikes than to injuries from pedal bikes, so families should think of an e-bike as more like a motor vehicle than a toy.
experts.who: Seth Weir, DO, Prisma Health (reported by Healio)

experts.say: Doctors see rising rates of child injuries and hospital stays from e-bikes, and they say better safety education and helmet use are needed.
experts.who: Laura Goodman, pediatric surgeon, Children's Hospital of Orange County (quoted by NPR)

future: Driving safely and patiently, with eyes on the road and the phone put away, so they can get to work, school, and church and help others do the same.
Caring for the machines they own, like checking tires, brakes, and chains, and knowing when something is not safe to use.
Understanding how wheels, gears, and motors work, which is the starting point for many jobs in building, repair, engineering, and farming.
Judging new kinds of wheels, such as e-bikes, scooters, and self-driving cars, by asking: Is it safe? Do I know the rules? Am I ready for it?
work: Wheels carry missionaries, ministers, and volunteers on bikes, buses, and cars, so the good news of Jesus Christ can reach people in their own towns and homes.
Wheels carry Bibles and printed scriptures in many languages to places where people have been waiting to read God's word.
Wheels bring food, medicine, wheelchairs, and ambulances to the poor, the sick, and the elderly, which is the kind of service Jesus taught in the parable of the Good Samaritan.
A family car can be a place to talk, sing, pray before a trip, and offer a ride to a neighbor who needs one, which strengthens families and friendships.
ldsWork: Missionaries of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints have long used bicycles and cars to go from home to home teaching about the Savior. Church leaders have taught that this gathering of Israel is the most important work happening on the earth today
Wheels help families travel to the temple so they can make sacred covenants and do ordinance work for their ancestors they found through family history.
The pioneer handcarts are part of Church history, and remembering them can help children learn faith, sacrifice, and care for one another as they get ready to welcome the Savior when He comes again.

bad: Writing lies about someone.
Writing cruel words that stay and hurt again and again.
Writing to trick people out of what is theirs.
items.why: Without writing there is no scripture. Writing is how Heavenly Father's words reached us across thousands of years, and how your family's stories will reach your grandchildren.

ages.0-2: Scribbles beside you; they learn that marks mean something.
ages.16+: Write the family's stories down; that is family history.
ages.3-5: Their own name, and letters they dictate to you.
ages.6-9: Thank-you notes and a first journal with pictures.
ages.10-12: A real journal, written weekly; letters that get a reply.
ages.13-15: Essays and, above all, a written testimony of their own.

good: Keeping the scriptures so every family can read them.
Writing a letter to someone who is sad.
Writing down what a child said so it is never lost.
harm: Hurtful words on a page or a screen last long after the anger is gone.
Written lies look like truth; children believe what is written down.
kids: Write only what you would say to someone's face.
Write true things.
Write something kind to someone every week.
items.name: Writing
items.talk: If you could write one true thing for your grandchildren to read, what would it be?
items.what: Marks that hold words. Once people could write, a thought could outlive the person who had it.
avoid: Writing anything you would not say to the person's face.
Sharing another person's secret in writing.
Copying someone else's words and calling them your own.
bless: Thank-you notes to teachers, leaders and grandparents.
A journal: the story of their life, kept for their own children.
Letters to a missionary, a soldier, or someone alone.
dangers: Written words can be copied and spread before they are checked.
A lie written well can look like truth.

learned.note: Every screen technology since is still writing: texts, posts and chat are words that stay. A child who learns 'written words last' is ready for all of them.

stages.0-2: Babies and toddlers aren't ready to write, but they are ready to be read to. Read aloud with your little one every day from birth, and let them scribble with chunky crayons, because cuddling up with a book helps their brain and their bond with you grow.
stages.3-5: Let your child draw, scribble, trace letters and learn to write their own name, and write down the stories they tell you so they see that marks can hold their words. Small hands are still getting strong, so keep it playful and short.
stages.6-8: This is the time to learn handwriting with a pencil and paper, and to write short notes, thank-you cards and simple journals. Children this age tend to believe whatever is written down, so start teaching them gently that kind words on a page last, and so do unkind ones.
stages.9-11: Children can write longer stories, letters to grandparents and journals, and can start learning to type, but they should keep writing by hand too. Help them ask "Who wrote this, and how do they know?" because they are now old enough to learn that not everything written is true.
stages.12-14: Young teens write a lot in texts, chats and posts, where a message sent in anger can be saved and shared forever. Talk together about pausing before sending, checking whether something is true before passing it on, and writing in a way they'd be glad for anyone to read.
stages.15-17: Teens should write essays, letters and journals in their own words to learn how to think clearly, even when computer tools such as AI can write for them. Help them treat those tools as helpers and not a replacement for their own thinking, and keep writing a regular habit as they get close to adulthood.
stages.18+: Young adults should write well and honestly at school, at work and online, because their written words speak for them and stay on record. Keeping a journal and writing to family can bless them and the people who come after them.

studies.finding: The American Academy of Pediatrics says parents should read aloud with their children starting at birth. Reading together often helps the bond between parent and child at an important time and helps build the brain.
studies.source: American Academy of Pediatrics, policy statement 'Literacy Promotion: An Essential Component of Primary Care Pediatric P

studies.finding: In a small brain-scan (EEG) study of 36 college students, writing words by hand linked up more parts of the brain than typing did, including parts tied to memory. This suggests that handwriting may help learning. The research is still early and was done with young adults, not children, and other scientists have published a formal response questioning parts of it.
studies.source: Van der Weel & Van der Meer, Frontiers in Psychology, reported by Science News

studies.finding: In a UK survey of almost 115,000 children aged 5 to 18, only about 1 in 4 said they enjoy writing in their free time, the lowest level since 2010. Just 1 in 10 said they write something for fun every day.
studies.source: National Literacy Trust, Annual Literacy Survey 2025

studies.finding: U.S. 12th graders' average reading score in 2024 was the lowest ever recorded on the national test, 10 points below the first test in 1992. Reading and writing grow together, so time spent reading at home matters.
studies.source: National Assessment of Educational Progress (The Nation's Report Card), Grade 12 Reading 2024

experts.say: There is a real difference in how the brain is organized for handwriting compared with typing. This adds to growing evidence that writing with a pen or pencil helps us learn and remember.
experts.who: Ramesh Balasubramaniam, neuroscientist, University of California, Merced (not involved in the study)

experts.say: Children enjoy writing much less than they used to, with a drop of nearly half over 15 years. The charity warns this could hurt learning and literacy in the long run.
experts.who: National Literacy Trust (UK literacy charity)

experts.say: Reading scores fell again in 2024 for both 4th and 8th graders, and the students who were already struggling fell further behind. Strong readers were mostly holding steady.
experts.who: Chalkbeat education reporting on National Assessment of Educational Progress results

future: Writing clearly and kindly: emails, reports and messages that others can understand and trust
Checking whether written information is true: knowing who wrote it, why, and how they know
Thinking for themselves on paper, and using computer writing tools such as AI wisely without letting those tools do their thinking
Keeping good records and taking good notes, by hand or by keyboard, for learning, work and family life
work: The scriptures are God's word written down, so they can be read in every land and in every age, and translating them into more languages lets more people read them in their own words.
Letters, notes and messages of love can comfort the sick, the lonely and those far from home, just as the apostles wrote letters to strengthen the early Saints.
Written records such as family journals, recipes, testimonies and stories pass faith and wisdom from parents to children and grandchildren.
Learning to read and write lifts people out of poverty, and teaching others to read is a way to serve them.
ldsWork: Church leaders have long taught members to keep personal journals and family records, so their testimonies and stories can bless their families and the generations after them.

Through FamilySearch, volunteers read old handwritten records such as births, marriages and censuses and turn them into searchable names, which helps families find their ancestors and take their names to the temple.

The Book of Mormon is itself a written record that was kept and preserved so it could come forth in the latter days. Translating it into many languages helps gather Israel and prepare the world for the Savior's return.

bad: Printing and passing around things that harm people.
Wasting it: paper is trees.
items.why: Paper made scripture light enough to carry and cheap enough to share. Every book on your shelf, including the bedtime books, stands on this Chinese invention.

ages.0-2: Board books; let them turn the pages.
ages.16+: Keep a paper journal for the things too sacred for a screen.
ages.3-5: Crayons and paper every day; a picture for grandma.
ages.6-9: Their own books, and a shelf to keep them on.
ages.10-12: Paper scriptures of their own, marked in their own hand.
ages.13-15: Study on paper as well as on a screen; it sticks better.

good: Books a family can afford.
Drawing and letters for someone who is far away.
Keeping records so that promises are kept.
harm: Very little. Paper is one of the safest gifts a child can be handed.
kids: Treat books gently; they are someone's work.
Use both sides.
A hand-written note is a gift.
items.name: Paper
items.talk: Why do we still love paper books when we have screens?
items.what: Thin sheets made from plant fibre. Cheap enough that ordinary people could own writing.
avoid: Tearing and wasting; teach that paper is a tree and a gift.
Reading only screens: paper rests the eyes and settles the mind.
bless: Handmade cards for the lonely.
A scrapbook of the family's year.
Wrap a gift with your own drawing on it.
dangers: Paper burns and rots; things kept only on paper can be lost.
Cheap copies made false ideas easy to spread too.

learned.note: Reading on paper still helps children remember more than reading the same words on a screen, in study after study. That is why the bedtime books are printed.

stages.0-2: Sturdy board books and big paper for scribbling are a gift at this age. Read them together on your lap. Little ones learn words by talking with you, and in one study, parents and toddlers talked more about the story with printed books than with e-books. Stay close, because babies put things in their mouths and may chew or swallow torn bits of paper.
stages.3-5: Give plenty of paper for drawing, tracing and writing letters by hand. Studies suggest that writing letters by hand helps young children learn to read and spell better than typing them. Keep scissors child-safe and keep reading printed picture books together.
stages.6-8: Let children write by hand every day: stories, thank-you notes and simple journals. Children this age are still tying sounds, shapes and hand movements together, and research suggests the hand does part of the teaching. Typing can come later and slowly.
stages.9-11: Keep printed books and handwritten notes in daily life even as schoolwork moves onto screens. Studies of children this age found they often understood a story better on paper, even though many liked screens more. Cursive, journals and a printed copy of the scriptures are good to have now.
stages.12-14: Teens this age can learn when paper works best, like taking notes by hand, planning and slow, careful reading, and when a screen is faster. Help them try both and notice which helps them remember. Their own judgment is growing, so talk it over with them instead of only setting rules.
stages.15-17: Older teens should be able to move easily between paper and screen. They might read long or hard material in print, write first drafts or study notes by hand, and type when speed matters. A handwritten letter or journal kept now can become a treasure to their own children someday.
stages.18+: Young adults choose for themselves. They do well to keep paper as a tool for deep reading, careful thinking, letters to loved ones and personal or family records, while using digital tools for work. Encourage them to keep their important papers safe and to write their own history.

studies.finding: In a study of Spanish-speaking children who could not yet read, those who practised letters and words by copying or tracing them by hand did better than those who typed, especially at spelling.
studies.source: Ibaibarriaga, Acha & Perea, Journal of Experimental Child Psychology (reported by PsyPost)

studies.finding: A review of 39 studies with 1,812 children found lower story comprehension when the same book was read on a screen instead of on paper. Digital books with good built-in features, like a dictionary, helped vocabulary, so the evidence is mixed rather than simple.
studies.source: Furenes, Kucirkova & Bus, Review of Educational Research (meta-analysis)

studies.finding: In a small study, parents and toddlers talked more, and talked more about the story, with print books than with e-books, where talk turned to the device. The authors suggested pediatricians recommend print books to families.
studies.source: Munzer et al., Pediatrics, reported in AAP News (American Academy of Pediatrics)

studies.finding: Fifth and sixth graders understood texts better on paper than on screen, even though most of them preferred screens. The researchers warned that the research on children is still fairly small.
studies.source: Golan, Barzillai & Katzir, Computers & Education

studies.finding: A recent review concludes that handwriting and typing do not work the same way in the brain. Handwriting seems to give special help while children are learning their letters, and typing works well once a child can already read and write.
studies.source: Digital Transition and Mental Health in School Settings: Does Handwriting Still Matter? (peer-reviewed review, PubMed Ce

experts.say: As handwriting gives way to keyboards, researchers who measured brain activity urge that children write by hand in school from an early age, because writing by hand lit up wider brain networks linked to memory and learning. Their study looked at young adults, so for children this is still a strong recommendation, not proof.
experts.who: Audrey van der Meer and Ruud van der Weel, Norwegian University of Science and Technology

experts.say: Typing is efficient once children can read and write, but handwriting gives a hands-on experience while children are first linking letters, movements and sounds. So schools that drop paper too early may lose something.
experts.who: Authors of a multidisciplinary peer-reviewed review

experts.say: Cursive is coming back in many U.S. public schools, and researchers are now studying how learning it affects children's reading and writing. The answers are still being worked out.
experts.who: Director of the Iowa Reading Research Center

experts.say: E-books are handy, but toddlers may get less from them than from print books. Parents who use e-books should read them the same warm, talk-together way they read print books.
experts.who: Pediatric researchers, in a study and commentary in Pediatrics
experts.source: AAP News, American Academy of Pediatrics

future: Writing clearly and neatly by hand, for notes, forms, signatures and personal letters
Deep, careful reading of long printed texts, and knowing when paper helps you understand better than a screen
Taking notes and planning by hand to think through ideas and remember them
Keeping and organizing important paper records, like certificates, contracts and family documents, and moving between paper and digital copies
work: Printed Bibles and scriptures in many languages let ordinary families read God's word for themselves, even where there is no electricity or internet.
Handwritten letters and cards carry comfort and love to the sick, the lonely, missionaries and people far from home.
Paper journals and family Bibles hold a family's faith, prayers and stories for children and grandchildren to read.
Simple printed lessons, hymnbooks and tracts help churches teach and serve people in poor or remote places at very low cost.
ldsWork: Family history rests largely on paper records like parish books, census pages and certificates. FamilySearch has worked for many years to gather and preserve these so members can find their ancestors' names and take them to the temple.

The Book of Mormon was first published as a printed book in 1830. Printed copies, translated into many languages, have helped carry the message of the Restoration and helped in what Church leaders call the gathering of Israel.

Church leaders have long encouraged members to keep personal journals and family histories. These records strengthen the faith of future generations and help turn the hearts of the children to their fathers.

bad: Printing lies faster than anyone can answer them.
Printing things that make people cruel or ashamed.
items.why: Before the press, a Bible cost more than a house. After it, ordinary families could read the scriptures in their own homes. A boy reading his own Bible in his own home is how the Restoration began.

ages.0-2: Board books, read aloud every day.
ages.16+: Publish something of their own; the press is theirs too.
ages.3-5: Picture books at bedtime, the same ones over and over; that is how they learn.
ages.6-9: Their own library card, books chosen together.
ages.10-12: Chapter books, and the first lesson in checking a claim: who wrote this, and how do they know?
ages.13-15: Read widely, the classics included, and learn to spot propaganda by its feel.

good: Scriptures in every home, in every language.
Books that teach children to read.
News that tells the truth to everyone at once.
harm: Printed lies look true; propaganda was printed on the same presses as scripture.
Books and magazines carry adult content into a home as easily as good words.
kids: Ask who wrote it and why.
Read the scriptures for yourself.
Just because it is printed does not make it true.
items.name: The Printing Press
items.talk: What would it be like if only one family in town owned a Bible?
items.what: A machine that presses inked letters onto paper, page after page. The first big book it printed was the Bible.
avoid: Books and magazines a parent has not looked at first.
Believing something because it is in print.
Comics and fan stories from unknown sources.
bless: Print a family book of your own stories.
Give scriptures to someone who has none.
Make a neighborhood newsletter that tells the good news.
dangers: Whoever owns the press decides what millions read.
Propaganda - printed lies - has started wars.

learned.note: Within fifty years of the press there were eight million books in Europe. Fifty years after the smartphone there are five billion of them. Both changed everything, faster than anyone planned for.

stages.0-2: Read sturdy picture books with your baby every day, even from birth, while they sit on your lap. Babies learn words and feel safe when they hear your voice and see pictures with you. Books are for sharing at this age, not for using alone.
stages.3-5: Read aloud each day, point at the pictures, and ask what might happen next. Pick the books yourself, because little ones believe whatever a page shows them and can't yet sort good words from bad.
stages.6-8: Children who are learning to read should read every day, both on their own and with you, from books you have looked at first. Begin to teach a simple rule: just because something is printed doesn't make it true, so we ask who wrote it and why.
stages.9-11: Let your child choose more of their own books and magazines, and check what they choose in a friendly way. Talk together about stories and ads. Children this age are building their tastes and can start comparing what different sources say.
stages.12-14: Encourage reading for fun and reading scripture alone. Explain that some printed things carry adult content or one-sided claims, and keep the door open so they'll tell you what they find. Young teens want more freedom but still need a parent close by.
stages.15-17: Teens can read widely, including hard books, news and other viewpoints. Help them check facts, compare sources and put down what hurts the spirit. They are learning to make their own choices, and guided practice now builds wisdom for later.
stages.18+: Young adults choose their own reading. Encourage the habit of reading deeply on paper, studying scripture daily and checking claims before passing them on. These habits help with study, work, faith and being a good citizen.

studies.finding: The American Academy of Pediatrics says children's doctors should encourage parents to read aloud with their children from birth and to choose books over screen entertainment for young children. Reading with children from infancy through the preschool years is linked to stronger language skills when school starts and better reading later.
studies.source: American Academy of Pediatrics, Literacy Promotion: An Essential Component of Primary Care Pediatric Practice (Pediatric

studies.finding: A 2025 review in The Journal of Pediatrics found a small but real advantage for understanding what you read on paper compared with screens. The effect is modest, and research is mixed. Younger children may be hurt more by screen reading, perhaps because they get distracted more easily.
studies.source: The Journal of Pediatrics, Paper versus Screen: The Unresolved Conflict in Children's and Adolescents' Learning Processe

studies.finding: A review of 39 studies with 1,812 children found that a grown-up talking with a child while reading a printed book helped the child understand more than the built-in extras in digital books did when children read those books alone.
studies.source: Furenes, Kucirkova & Bus, Review of Educational Research (meta-analysis)

studies.finding: A 2025 study looked at 20 years of U.S. time-use data, from 2003 to 2023, to track reading for pleasure and reading with children. It found that reading for pleasure has gone down a lot over those two decades.
studies.source: iScience, The decline in reading for pleasure over 20 years of the American Time Use Survey

experts.say: The 2025 Annual Literacy Survey of almost 115,000 UK children found that only 1 in 3 children aged 8 to 18 enjoy reading in their free time, and only 1 in 5 read something every day. Both are the lowest numbers in 20 years.
experts.who: National Literacy Trust
experts.source: National Literacy Trust, Children and young people's reading in 2025

experts.say: Reading for fun helps children build imagination and care for others, but fewer children are doing it. By middle school, only about 1 in 7 read for pleasure each day.
experts.who: Education researchers writing in The Conversation
experts.source: The Conversation, Reading for pleasure builds empathy in children, but fewer kids are picking up books just for the fun

experts.say: New U.S. Department of Education data show the share of 9- and 13-year-olds who read for fun almost every day has dropped by double digits. The same children's reading scores have also fallen since 2012.
experts.who: U.S. Department of Education data, reported by NBC News

experts.say: As of August 1, 2025, only 544 of the world's 7,396 living languages were still waiting for Bible translation to begin.
experts.who: Wycliffe Global Alliance

future: Reading long, hard texts with focus, which helps in school, at work and in scripture study.
Checking whether something printed is true: who wrote it, why they wrote it, and what other trusted sources say.
Writing clearly so that others can understand you and are helped by what you write.
Choosing good books and turning away from harmful ones, even when no one else is watching.
work: It puts the Bible into people's hands in their own language. The complete Bible is now printed in more than 800 languages, and translation goes on every year.
It lets families keep printed scriptures, storybooks and hymnbooks at home to read together every day.
It spreads reading. People who can read can learn about Jesus Christ for themselves and also find work, health help and hope.
It lets churches and caring groups print simple guides, lessons and notes of comfort for the poor, the sick and the lonely.
ldsWork: President M. Russell Ballard taught that the Lord inspired Johannes Gutenberg's printing press as a monumental step in preparing the world for the Restoration of the gospel (Ensign, January 2020, churchofjesuschrist.org/study/ensign/2020/01/how-the-lord-prepar

Church history lessons teach that printing made the Bible widely available, and that making the scriptures available and helping God's children learn to read them helped prepare the way for the Restoration (churchofjesuschrist.org, Prelude to the Restoration).
Printed scriptures, including the Book of Mormon, help carry the restored gospel to people around the world. Printed records and family histories also help families learn about their ancestors.

bad: Spying on people who want to be left alone.
Aiming weapons from far away.
items.why: The heavens declare the glory of God, and the telescope let us read that declaration. The same glass, turned the other way, became the microscope and showed the tiny worlds that keep us alive.

ages.16+: Teach a younger child the sky.
ages.3-5: The moon and the bright planets through binoculars on a parent's lap.
ages.6-9: A small telescope with a grown-up; learn the moon's face.
ages.10-12: Find Jupiter's moons the way Galileo did.
ages.13-15: Learn the constellations and how far the light has come.

good: Learning how big and orderly Heavenly Father's creation is.
Finding ships in trouble at sea.
Microscopes that find sickness so doctors can heal it.
harm: Only one: never point it at the sun.
kids: Look up at night; wonder is a gift.
Use it to learn, not to spy.
Share what you see.
items.name: The Telescope
items.talk: When you look at the stars, what do you think Heavenly Father wants you to feel?
items.what: Curved glass that brings far things close. Galileo pointed one at the sky and saw moons around Jupiter.
avoid: Looking at the sun through any lens.
Buying a toy telescope that shows nothing; a good pair of binoculars is better.
bless: Show a friend the moon's craters for the first time.
Let wonder turn into gratitude: 'the heavens declare the glory of God.'
Star-gaze with the family on a clear night and read Abraham 3 or Psalm 8.
dangers: Never look at the sun through one; it can blind you in a second.

learned.note: Every telescope since Galileo has found more order, not less. The sky is still the easiest place to feel small and loved at the same time.

stages.0-2: Babies and toddlers should not use a telescope. They can't yet follow a safety rule like 'never at the sun,' so just hold them and look up at the moon and stars together with your own eyes.
stages.3-5: Young children can peek through the eyepiece at night while a grown-up aims it and holds it steady. They are still learning to follow rules, so keep the cover on during the day and keep the telescope stored out of reach.
stages.6-8: At this age a child can help find the moon or a bright planet at night with a parent right there. Teach them one firm rule they can say back to you: the sun can hurt your eyes forever, so we never look at it through a telescope.
stages.9-11: Children this age can learn to set up and aim a telescope on their own at night and keep a simple notebook of what they see. Check on them now and then, because eye doctors reported real sun-damage cases in children 8 to 11 after the 2024 eclipse.
stages.12-14: Young teens can use a telescope on their own at night and may enjoy a local astronomy club or school night-sky event. Any daytime sun viewing should use a proper solar filter on the front of the telescope, and only with an adult checking it.
stages.15-17: Teens can learn to look after a telescope, take photos through it, and help younger brothers and sisters use it safely. They are also ready to understand bigger questions, like how light from satellites is making the sky harder to study.
stages.18+: Young adults can use telescopes freely and safely and may study astronomy, physics, or engineering, where these skills lead to real jobs. They can also teach others how to observe safely and help with research that anyone can join.

studies.finding: Never look at the sun through a telescope, binoculars, or camera without a proper solar filter, even if you are wearing eclipse glasses. Even a short look can permanently damage the back of the eye (the retina). Sunglasses are not enough.
studies.source: American Academy of Ophthalmology, Solar Eclipse Eye Safety

studies.finding: Eye doctors in Quebec confirmed cases of sun damage to the retina after the April 8, 2024 eclipse. Some of the damaged eyes showed a pattern already described in children, and the doctors concluded that the risk from eclipse viewing is real.
studies.source: Canadian Journal of Ophthalmology, 'Solar retinopathy following the April 2024 eclipse in Quebec, Canada'

studies.finding: A nationwide U.S. review found no significant rise in emergency room visits for eye pain or sun-burned eyes after the 2024 eclipse. It is good news that serious injuries seem uncommon when people are warned. However, the authors note that their method may have missed some retina injuries, so the evidence is mixed rather than settled.
studies.source: Incidence of Solar Retinopathy and Photokeratitis in US Emergency Departments Surrounding the April 2024 Total Solar Ecl

experts.say: Telescopes and binoculars focus the sun's rays even more strongly than our eyes do. That is why looking at the sun through one without a filter can cause serious eye injury, even if you are wearing eclipse glasses.
experts.who: Dr. Russell Van Gelder, clinical spokesman for the American Academy of Ophthalmology

experts.say: Light from the huge number of satellites planned for Earth's orbit could spoil most pictures taken by some space telescopes. The researchers propose steps to predict and correct this problem.
experts.who: NASA-led team of astronomers
experts.source: Nature, 'Satellite megaconstellations will threaten space-based astronomy'

experts.say: The same satellites that bring internet to rural and remote places around the world are also adding to light pollution. That light could affect about 40% of Hubble images. One tool can both bless people and make other work harder.
experts.who: NASA researchers, as reported by Reuters

future: Careful observing and record-keeping: noticing small details, writing down what you see, and checking it again later. Science, medicine, and many trades rely on this skill.
Safety judgment with powerful tools: knowing what a tool can do to your body before you use it, and following safety rules even when no one is watching.
Understanding light, lenses, and images. These ideas are used in cameras, eyeglasses, microscopes, phones, and medical scanners.
Reading data and images from big telescopes and satellites, and judging whether a claim about space is backed by real evidence.
work: Looking through a telescope at the moon and stars can help children feel wonder at the size and beauty of creation, which leads naturally to gratitude and prayer: 'The heavens declare the glory of God' (Psalm 19:1).
The science of lenses that began with the telescope also gave us microscopes, eyeglasses, and cameras. Doctors and nurses use these to help the sick and the poor see and heal.
Satellites, which came from the same science of watching the sky, help carry the scriptures and messages of hope to faraway places in many languages.
A family stargazing night is a simple way to put screens down, talk together, and teach children to use God-given tools carefully and safely.
ldsWork: Latter-day Saint scripture teaches that God has created 'worlds without number' and that He knows them all (Moses 1:33-35). Looking through a telescope can help children feel how great His work is, and how much He knows and loves each of His children. https://

The Lord showed Abraham the stars and taught him about the order of the heavens (Abraham 3). Watching the sky with a telescope is a gentle way to teach this scripture as a family. https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/scriptures/pgp/abr/3?lang=eng

The Lord taught that whoever has seen the earth, the sun, the moon, and the stars has 'seen God moving in his majesty and power' (Doctrine and Covenants 88:45-47). A telescope can help children see that majesty more clearly. https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org

bad: Factories that worked small children twelve hours a day.
Smoke that made whole cities sick.
items.why: Steam shrank the world. Missionaries crossed oceans in weeks instead of months, and the Saints crossed a continent to gather. Work that broke backs could be done by a machine, so children could go to school.

ages.16+: Repair and build; machines as a way to serve.
ages.3-5: Toy engines and a museum visit.
ages.6-9: Take a simple machine apart with a grown-up.
ages.10-12: Help with tools, with safety glasses and supervision.
ages.13-15: Learn a power tool properly, from a parent.

good: Trains that bring families together across a country.
Pumping clean water into cities.
Factories that make warm clothes cheap enough for everyone.
harm: Machines do not stop for a hand or a foot.
kids: Machines should make people's lives better, not people smaller.
Rest is not laziness.
Thank the people who keep the engines running.
items.name: The Steam Engine
items.talk: If a machine could do your chores, what would you do with the time?
items.what: Boiling water pushes a piston, and the piston turns a wheel. Trains, ships and factories that never got tired.
avoid: Playing near running machinery or engines.
Treating a lawn mower or a power tool as a toy.
bless: Learn how a machine works, then fix one for someone who cannot.
Mow, plow or haul for a neighbor with the machine you have.
dangers: A boiler that is not watched can explode.
When machines do the work, people can be treated like machines.

learned.note: It took laws, not machines, to get children out of the factories. A new tool does not decide how it is used; people do.

stages.0-2: Babies and toddlers can enjoy picture books and toy trains, but they should never be near real tractors, mowers, trains or other big machines. They move quickly, they can't yet understand danger, and in one study of tractor injuries, children 4 and under had the most serious injuries.
stages.3-5: Young children can watch a train or a working machine from a safe place while holding a grown-up's hand. They should never ride on a mower or tractor, because children who ride along often walk up to the machine later, when it can hurt them.
stages.6-8: Early elementary children can learn simple rules like "See tracks? Think train!" and cross tracks only where there are signs or gates. They are ready to learn how steam pushes a piston, but not to run any machine.
stages.9-11: Older children can visit a museum steam engine or a heritage railway and learn how it works, while staying behind the rope and close to an adult. They may want to help with grown-up jobs to please their parents, so parents should choose tasks that fit the child's age.
stages.12-14: Young teens can learn real safety habits, such as keeping hands away from moving parts, never removing guards, and staying at least 15 feet from railroad tracks. In the U.S., they should not drive tractors or farm machines unless they have finished a certified safety course and an adult is watching.
stages.15-17: Teens can begin learning to run machines with training, steady supervision and enough rest, because tiredness and rushing lead to injuries. They should never try to beat a train or go around crossing lights and gates.
stages.18+: Young adults can work with engines and machines in trades, farming, transport and engineering. They should keep using the safety habits they learned and teach them to younger children.

studies.finding: A study of tractor injuries at four trauma centers in the U.S. Midwest found that children 4 and under had the most serious injuries and the longest stays in intensive care. The littlest children need to be kept well away from working machines.
studies.source: Sang et al., Journal of Agromedicine, "Tractor injuries in the upper Midwestern United States"

studies.finding: A University of Iowa study found that most serious lawn mower injuries to children happened to bystanders struck by the mower. Most of those children (73%) had ridden on a mower before as a passenger. Letting a child ride along can teach them to come close to the machine later.
studies.source: University of Iowa Injury Prevention Research Center

studies.finding: A study of farm tractor deaths in Iceland from 1918 to 2024 found that the death rate for children was more than four times higher than for adults. It notes that U.S. rules do not allow children under 16 to run tractors unless they work on their parents' farm or have finished a certified safety program.
studies.source: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, "Child Fatalities in Tractor-Related Accidents in Rur

studies.finding: Rail safety guidance: cross tracks only at marked crossings, stay at least 15 feet from the rails, and never try to beat a train. A train can need a mile or more to stop.
studies.source: Operation Lifesaver, Inc.

experts.say: Children's injuries on farms should not be called "accidents," because they can be prevented. About 33 children are hurt on U.S. farms every day, and most deaths involve tractors and other machinery.
experts.who: National Farm Medicine Center (Marshfield Clinic Research Institute)

experts.say: Keeping children safe around farm machines needs help at every level: families, communities, states and the nation. A national action plan sets goals for doing this.
experts.who: National Children's Center for Rural and Agricultural Health and Safety
experts.source: Safeguarding Children in Agriculture: A National Action Plan 2025

experts.say: Busy seasons like Halloween, fall festivals and the holidays bring more families outdoors near tracks. Everyone should take care, because trains cannot stop quickly.
experts.who: Operation Lifesaver, Inc., the largest rail safety education group in the U.S.

future: Safety habits around any engine or moving machine: keep guards on, turn the machine off before reaching in, and stay out of its path.
Understanding how heat and pressure become motion, which is the basis for engineering, power plants, cars and modern trades.
Being safe around transport, such as trains, crossings and vehicles, and knowing how far big machines need to stop.
Training others with patience and care, and fitting each job to the person's age and skill, whether at work or at home.
work: Trains and steamships let missionaries and Bibles travel faster and farther, so more people could hear the good news of Jesus Christ.
Steam-powered printing presses made books cheaper, so more families could have the scriptures in their own language.
Railways carried food, medicine and help to the poor and the sick in faraway places.
Faster travel helped scattered families visit, write and gather together, so family ties stayed strong.

bad: Pictures taken to embarrass or shame someone.
Pictures that show what should stay private.
Faked pictures that tell lies.
items.why: A photograph lets a child see the great-grandmother who prayed for them. Family history became something you could hold. Every face in your scrapbook is here because of this.

ages.0-2: Parents take the photos and keep them private.
ages.16+: Become the family's photographer and historian.
ages.3-5: Hold the family camera with a parent; photos stay in the family.
ages.6-9: A simple camera of their own; nothing shared online.
ages.10-12: No camera phone in a bedroom; ask before sharing any picture of a person.
ages.13-15: The rule that never bends: no photo of your body to anyone, and no photo kept secret from parents.

good: Remembering the people we love, exactly as they were.
Showing the truth of something that happened far away.
A picture for someone who cannot be there.
harm: A photo shared can never be taken back; it can be copied, changed and used against them.
Constant comparison with edited pictures of other people's lives.
Predators ask for pictures first.
kids: Ask before you take someone's picture.
Never share a picture that would embarrass someone.
If a picture makes you feel yucky, tell a grown-up.
items.name: Photography
items.talk: Which photograph in our house means the most to you, and why?
items.what: Light on a treated plate makes a picture of exactly what was there. For the first time a face could be kept.
avoid: Sharing a photo of a friend without asking them.
Any photo in a bathroom, bedroom or swimsuit sent to anyone.
Sending a picture to someone you have not met in person.
bless: Photograph the family's history: grandparents, homes, headstones, hands.
Send pictures to a grandparent every Sunday.
Take the pictures at a service project so the story can be told.
dangers: A photo can be copied forever and shown to anyone.
Some pictures are not meant for children's eyes, and they arrive without warning.

learned.note: Today a phone takes a hundred pictures where a plate took one. The rule did not change: a picture is a gift when it is kept for love and a weapon when it is used for shame.

stages.0-2: Babies and toddlers do not need to take pictures. They learn by touching, looking and being held, so let them be in family photos, keep those photos private, and leave out bath-time pictures and anything that shows where they live or go to school.
stages.3-5: Young children can take pictures of their toys, pets and flowers with a grown-up nearby, and they can look at family photos while hearing the stories behind them. They are just starting to learn that their body belongs to them, so teach them that no one should ask for pictures of their body and that they should always tell you if someone does.
stages.6-8: Children this age can take and keep pictures on a family device, but they should not share them online on their own. They are learning about rules and about being fair, so teach them to ask 'May I take your picture?' and 'May I share it?' and to come to you if anyone online asks for a photo.
stages.9-11: Older children can learn real photography skills like framing, light and simple editing, and they can make family or school projects, with a parent approving anything that gets shared. They are starting to compare themselves with others, so show them how pictures get edited and filtered, and tell them often that they will never be in trouble for telling you about a scary message.
stages.12-14: Young teens can share pictures with people they know in real life, using private accounts and with their parents checking in. This is the age when how they look and what friends think matter most to them, so talk often about edited and fake pictures, and set one firm rule: never send a picture of your body, even to someone you trust, and come to a parent right away if someone threatens you.
stages.15-17: Teens can grow into skilled and careful photographers and editors with less checking from parents, but keep talking with them. Their judgment is still growing, and older teens, boys especially, are a main target for photo scams that end in threats, so remind them that a threat is a crime against them, not their fault, and that you will help them report it.
stages.18+: Young adults can use photography fully in their work, service and family life. Help them build lasting habits: get consent before they share someone's picture, protect their own privacy, and be honest about when a picture has been changed or made by AI.

studies.finding: A University of Southampton survey of more than 1,000 UK parents found that 45% post their children's photos and information online ('sharenting'). One in six said their child had faced at least one harm such as cyberbullying, harassment, identity theft, privacy breaches or contact from a stranger. The researchers found a link but did not prove that the posts caused these harms. Posting less, and
studies.source: University of Southampton news release on sharenting research

studies.finding: A 2025 research summary found that among social media, photo-based platforms do the most harm to how young people feel about their bodies. Likes and comments on photos make that effect stronger or weaker, and taking selfies and using filters can affect body satisfaction from the preteen years into young adulthood. Much of this research shows links rather than causes, so it is still developing.
studies.source: Children and Screens: Institute of Digital Media and Child Development, 'Digital Media Use and Youth Body Image' Researc

studies.finding: Thorn surveyed young people aged 13 to 20 in the U.S. Many said that people who see a fake nude picture made with AI believe it is real, and many said such a picture cannot be fully removed from the internet. Of the respondents who said they had made these fake pictures, about 1 in 3 had made one of a minor. This shows why children should learn early that pictures can be faked and that making or s
studies.source: Thorn, 'Deepfake Nudes & Young People' (March 2025)

studies.finding: The U.S. Treasury's FinCEN says sextortion often involves adults pressuring minors into sending explicit pictures. It names boys aged 14 to 17 as an especially vulnerable group and tells people to report it at 1-800-CALL-FBI or tips.fbi.gov.
studies.source: FinCEN Notice on Financially Motivated Sextortion

experts.say: Sextortion can move very fast and is growing. The FBI says anyone targeted should stop responding, tell a trusted adult and report it. Parents should talk with their children ahead of time so the children feel safe coming forward.
experts.who: FBI agents in Texas

experts.say: An FBI spokesperson warned that photo-based sextortion 'happens in seconds.' Teenage boys are often the targets, and children as young as seven have been victims.
experts.who: Shelley Lynch, FBI Public Affairs Officer

experts.say: Researchers say their findings on parents sharing children's photos should be a wake-up call for regulators, because children face risks from these posts both now and later in life.
experts.who: Professor Pamela Ugwudike, University of Southampton

experts.say: Researchers who study children and media find that pictures, filters and online feedback shape how children see themselves. They point to media literacy and supportive adults as the way forward, rather than fear.
experts.who: Children and Screens: Institute of Digital Media and Child Development
experts.source: Digital Media and Youth Body Image

future: Telling real pictures from edited or AI-made ones, and checking a picture before believing it or passing it on.
Taking clear, honest photos and videos for school, work, small businesses, service projects and telling stories.
Protecting privacy: knowing what a photo can reveal, such as a location, a face or a school, and asking for consent before sharing someone's picture.
Keeping and organizing family photos and records so they last and can be shared with relatives.
work: Photos and videos can carry the message of Jesus Christ, and the people who live it, to people far away and in many languages, so they can see faith lived out and not only read about it.
Pictures can show the real needs of the poor, the sick and people hit by disaster, so that others are moved to give and help, as long as those pictures are shared with care and with permission.
Family photos help children know where they came from, remember loved ones who have died, and feel part of a family that loves them.
Pictures of baptisms, weddings, missions and quiet everyday kindness can strengthen faith and help families remember God's goodness to them.

bad: Spreading panic before the facts are known.
Sending orders to hurt people, fast.
items.why: The first message ever sent was a scripture: 'What hath God wrought' (Numbers 23:23). Distance stopped being a wall. Good news, and the gospel, could travel as fast as lightning.

ages.16+: Use the fastest word for the kindest reasons.
ages.3-5: Tap a code on the table: two taps means 'hello'.
ages.6-9: Learn the alphabet in Morse for fun.
ages.10-12: Understand that every text is a telegraph, and every telegraph is read by someone.
ages.13-15: Check a message before you pass it on.

good: Calling for help fast in an emergency.
Telling a family far away that everyone is safe.
Sending truth faster than a rumour can walk.
harm: Rumors travel as fast as truth once messages fly.
kids: Fast is not the same as true.
Wait before you pass something on.
Use it to say 'I am safe' and 'I love you'.
items.name: The Telegraph
items.talk: If you could send one message to anyone in the world right now, who would it be and what would it say?
items.what: Electric pulses down a wire, tapped out as dots and dashes. A message across a country in a minute instead of a month.
avoid: Passing on a message you have not checked.
bless: A quick word of comfort can reach across the world in a second; send one.
Learn Morse code together; tap out 'I love you.'
dangers: The faster news moves, the less time anyone has to check it.
Whoever controls the wire controls what people hear.

learned.note: The telegraph made the first 'breaking news'. People in 1850 complained that it made them anxious and hurried. It is not a new feeling.

stages.0-2: Babies and toddlers don't need fast messages at all. They learn trust and words from a parent's face, voice and arms, so let the only 'signals' be your own taps and lullabies.
stages.3-5: Little ones can play a tapping game with a parent, like 'two taps means I love you.' At this age a child believes almost everything they hear, so a grown-up should always be there to say what is true.
stages.6-8: Children this age love secret codes, so learning a few Morse code letters makes a fun family game. This is also a good time to start the habit of asking 'Is this true, and who told us?' Research shows that even young school children get better at spotting made-up stories when someone teaches them.
stages.9-11: Older children can send short coded or written messages to family and trusted friends while a parent can see them. Teach them to stop before passing anything on, because a false story can spread faster than a true one.
stages.12-14: Young teens can use quick messages more on their own, with clear family rules about when, where and with whom. Before they get more freedom, teach them how to check where a message came from, because feelings run strong at this age and rumors can hurt friends.
stages.15-17: Teens can handle fast messaging mostly on their own. Limits should still protect sleep, schoolwork and time with family. Parents can keep coaching them to check before sharing and to send kind, truthful words.
stages.18+: Young adults are free to use fast messages fully for school, work, mission service and family. They should keep the habits they practiced at home: check before you share, and let what you send be something you'd be glad for others to see.

studies.finding: In a very large study of messages shared online, false news spread 'farther, faster, deeper, and more broadly than the truth.' False stories were 70 percent more likely to be passed on, and people, not computer programs, did most of the spreading. This is the old telegraph lesson: a fast tool carries a rumor as easily as the truth.
studies.source: Vosoughi, Roy & Aral, Science (reported by MIT Sloan)

studies.finding: Elementary school children could often tell real news from fake news, and a short lesson on asking whether a story makes sense and where it came from helped them do better. This is early research, but it suggests that teaching children to check is worth the time.
studies.source: Shtulman et al., 'Children's detection of online misinformation,' Cognition 265

studies.finding: In UK surveys, about two in three children (68%) said they had seen misleading content online in a six-month period. In 2025 research, 27% said they had believed a fake or AI-made news story. The researchers advise helping children learn to question what they see and check it against trusted sources.
studies.source: Internet Matters

studies.finding: The American Academy of Pediatrics advises families to make a Family Media Plan, to model healthy habits, and to use the '5 Cs': think about the child, the content, staying calm, what media crowds out, and talking together.
studies.source: American Academy of Pediatrics, 'Digital Ecosystems, Children, and Adolescents' (HealthyChildren.org)

studies.finding: The American Psychological Association advises that teens be trained in media literacy before they start using social media, and that use should not crowd out sleep or physical activity.
studies.source: American Psychological Association, Health Advisory on Social Media Use in Adolescence

experts.say: False stories spread faster than true ones mostly because people choose to pass them on. That means each of us, children included, can help slow a rumor by pausing before we share.
experts.who: Soroush Vosoughi, Deb Roy and Sinan Aral, MIT

experts.say: Most platforms are built to keep people using them and to earn money, not to help children grow well. Pediatricians are asking companies to design tools that are better for children.
experts.who: American Academy of Pediatrics

experts.say: Seeing misleading content can leave children trusting the news less and feeling confused and anxious. Learning to check information builds their confidence.
experts.who: Internet Matters researchers

experts.say: Quick, connected messaging can do real good, especially by keeping young people in touch during hard or lonely times. How it affects each child depends on the child and how they use it.
experts.who: American Psychological Association

future: Checking a message before believing or sharing it: who sent it, does it make sense, and what do trusted sources say?
Writing short, clear, kind messages that say exactly what you mean, a skill every job and family needs.
Knowing how messages travel through wires and signals, the first step toward understanding modern networks and computers.
Choosing when to answer and when to put the device down, so fast messages serve your life instead of running it.
work: Good news can travel as fast as bad news. A message of hope in Jesus Christ can reach a faraway friend in moments.
Quick messages help churches and neighbors gather help fast when someone is sick, hungry or hit by a disaster.
Families who live far apart can share love, prayers and news quickly, which helps keep hearts close.
Translators and Bible teachers in many lands can share and check their work quickly, which helps bring the scriptures to more people in their own language.
ldsWork: Church leaders have taught that the Lord inspires inventions so His work can go forward. Elder David A. Bednar's message 'To Sweep the Earth as with a Flood' invites members to use technology to share the gospel and to fill it with truth and goodness.
