Fast messages and the networks that grew from the telegraph help families share records and stories, so they can find their ancestors and take their names to the temple, which is part of turning hearts to the fathers.

Quick communication helps missionaries and members reach people in every nation. Church leaders teach that this is part of gathering Israel and preparing the world for the Savior's return, without saying when that day will come.

bad: Calls that scare or trick people, especially the elderly.
Talking on it while you should be with the people in front of you.
items.why: A grandmother's voice at bedtime from a thousand miles away. A prophet's voice reaching every home at once. The telephone gave families a way to stay close when life spread them out.

ages.0-2: Video calls so family faces stay familiar.
ages.16+: Their phone, their manners, their calls of service.
ages.3-5: Talk to grandma on speaker with you.
ages.6-9: Use the family phone with permission; learn to answer politely.
ages.10-12: A basic phone that calls and texts, only if truly needed, and only known numbers.
ages.13-15: Call etiquette; never answer or call strangers; the phone sleeps outside the bedroom.

good: Hearing the voice of someone you miss.
Calling a doctor or the fire department fast.
Checking on a neighbour who lives alone.
harm: Strangers can call a child; scammers call everyone.
Late-night calls steal sleep and privacy.
kids: Never give your name or address to a caller you do not know.
Put it down when someone is talking to you.
Call Grandma.
items.name: The Telephone
items.talk: Whose voice would you most like to hear tonight?
items.what: A voice turned into electricity and back into a voice. For the first time you could hear someone who was not in the room.
avoid: Giving a name, an address or a family's plans to any caller.
Answering unknown numbers alone.
Calls after the family's bedtime.
bless: Call grandparents every week; it is the call they wait for.
Check on a lonely neighbor or a widow by phone.
Be the one who calls to say sorry.
dangers: Anyone can call a child; not everyone who calls is a friend.
A phone can interrupt every meal and every bedtime if you let it.

learned.note: Phone scams now take billions of dollars a year, mostly from older people. Teaching grandparents 'hang up and call back' is a real act of love.

stages.0-2: Babies and toddlers can see and hear loving family on a video call, but only with a parent holding them and talking along. Doctors make an exception for video calls at this age because they are a real back-and-forth with people who love the child, and other screens are best avoided.
stages.3-5: Little children can talk with grandparents and other close family on the phone while a parent sits close by. This is a good age to start learning a parent's name and phone number and how to call for help in an emergency, because young children learn best by practicing with a grown-up.
stages.6-8: Children this age can make calls to family on a family phone with a parent's say-so. They should not answer calls from numbers they don't know, and they should learn to tell a grown-up about any call that felt strange. Children this age are still learning who to trust, so grown-ups should check first.
stages.9-11: Older children can call family and friends on a family phone or a simple phone. It's best to leave it outside the bedroom at night, because one study found that alerts going off at night woke many children this age. They are ready to learn a simple rule: never give out names, addresses or passwords on a call, and hang up when someone rushes or frightens you.
stages.12-14: Many children get their own phone at this age. It works best with parent-approved contacts, a family 'phone parks in the kitchen at night' rule, and talks about scams and strangers. Young teens want more independence but still need help guarding their sleep and their privacy.
stages.15-17: Teens can be given more freedom while still keeping phones out of the bedroom at night. They should practice grown-up calls, such as making a doctor's appointment, calling about a job, or calling a known number back to check whether a 'family emergency' call is real. These years are for building judgment that will soon be all their own.
stages.18+: Young adults manage their own phones. They do well when they guard their sleep, are wary of calls that rush them, and keep calling the people they love, because hearing a voice still builds closeness in a way a short text often can't.

studies.finding: The American Academy of Pediatrics and the World Health Organization advise no screen time for babies under 18 months, with one exception: video chatting with family or caregivers, because it is an interactive, social conversation. (This summary comes from a pediatric practice that reports the AAP and WHO guidance.)
studies.source: Blueberry Pediatrics, summarizing AAP and WHO guidance

studies.finding: A University of Toronto study in the journal Sleep Health found that more than 70% of tweens had an internet-connected device in their bedroom, and nearly a quarter said notifications had woken them in the past week. Bedtime device use was linked with more sleep problems. The study shows a link between the two, not proof that one causes the other.
studies.source: News-Medical, reporting on a study in Sleep Health (University of Toronto)

studies.finding: In experiments by researchers at the University of Texas at Austin and the University of Chicago, people expected a phone call to feel awkward, so they chose to type instead. In fact, hearing a voice created a stronger sense of connection than text did, without being more awkward. This is one research team's findings in adults, not a rule for children.
studies.source: UT News, University of Texas at Austin (Kumar & Epley, Journal of Experimental Psychology)

studies.finding: In reports to the U.S. Federal Trade Commission for 2025, 11% of people who lost money said the scam began with a phone call. Websites, apps and social media were now even more common starting points. That is why teaching children to be careful matters on every device, not just on the phone.
studies.source: Federal Trade Commission, Data Spotlight

experts.say: Phone scams still do a great deal of harm. For older adults, the typical amount lost per person was highest when a scam began with a phone call. These reports were made by the people affected and do not come from a survey.
experts.who: U.S. Federal Trade Commission

experts.say: Scammers now use computer-made voices that sound like a grandchild or other relative in trouble, so a scared family member will send money. The safe step is to hang up and call the loved one back on a number you already know.
experts.who: U.S. Federal Trade Commission (as reported in the news)
experts.source: GeekSpin, reporting on an FTC warning

experts.say: Calling more often could do people good. Researchers found that people tend to pick texting over calling because they expect a call to feel awkward, when a voice call actually makes them feel closer.
experts.who: Amit Kumar (University of Texas at Austin) and Nicholas Epley (University of Chicago)

future: Speaking clearly and kindly on a call: introducing yourself, asking for help, making an appointment, and doing a job interview by phone or video.
Spotting a scam: noticing when a caller rushes you, asks you to keep a secret, or wants gift cards or money, then hanging up and checking with a number you already know.
Guarding privacy: knowing what never to share on a call, such as passwords, codes, home address or account numbers.
Setting limits: knowing when to put the phone away, so it serves your sleep, your work and the people in front of you instead of ruling them.
work: Hearing a loved one's voice from far away strengthens families: a grandparent's 'I love you,' a parent's comfort, a child's 'goodnight' when someone is traveling.
A simple phone call lets us check on the sick, the lonely and the elderly, and lets us call for help in an emergency. It is a quiet way to love our neighbor.
The phone helps people share the good news of Jesus Christ and pray together across miles, and it can carry the scriptures to people who listen rather than read.
Volunteers, churches and charities use the phone to serve the poor: setting up meals, rides and visits for people who need them.
ldsWork: Missionaries today may call and video chat with their families each week, a change Church leaders made so families can stay close while missionaries help gather Israel.

Families can call grandparents and older relatives to hear and record their stories. Those stories can be kept in FamilySearch Memories, which turns family history into something a child can hear and love.
Leaders and members use calls to minister to one another, checking on members and arranging help and temple trips. This lets them follow the Savior's pattern of caring for the one.

bad: Lights that never go off, so nobody rests.
Bright screens and lights in the bedroom that keep children awake.
items.why: Light is the oldest sign of Heavenly Father's work: 'Let there be light.' Electric light let families read, study and gather after the sun went down, safely, and it lit the hospitals and schools that followed.

ages.16+: Keep their own dark, quiet hour before sleep.
ages.3-5: Lights off means eyes closed; keep the rule kindly.
ages.6-9: A reading lamp and a bedtime, both kept.
ages.10-12: No screens for an hour before bed; the light itself is the problem.
ages.13-15: Learn why blue light steals sleep, then choose.

good: Reading the scriptures together after dark.
Hospitals that can work through the night.
Streets that are safe to walk at night.
harm: Light at night, especially from screens, tells the body it is day; sleep suffers, and so does everything sleep protects.
kids: Lights off when you leave the room.
Dark room, better sleep.
Never touch a plug with wet hands.
items.name: The Electric Light
items.talk: Why do you think the very first thing created was light?
items.what: A glowing wire inside a glass bulb. Night stopped being dark, in every room, at the flip of a switch.
avoid: Bright screens and lights in the bedroom after dark.
Leaving every light on; a child should know light costs something.
bless: A lamp for reading scriptures together at night.
Leave a porch light on for someone coming home late.
Bring a flashlight and a meal to a neighbor whose power is out.
dangers: Electricity can hurt you: water and outlets do not mix.
Too much light at night confuses the body's clock and steals sleep.

learned.note: Children sleep better and longer in a dark room, and the blue light of screens at bedtime pushes sleep later. Dim the lights an hour before bed and the body does the rest.

stages.0-2: Keep the room dim and calm after dark. At night feedings, use only a small, low light and keep screens away from your baby. A baby's body clock is still learning when night is, and light is the strongest signal that it is daytime.
stages.3-5: Turn the lights down low for the last hour before bed, and keep screens out of bedtime. In small studies, even dim evening light sharply lowered the sleep hormone in preschoolers. Bright daytime light and outdoor play help the body clock grow strong.
stages.6-8: Let children help you turn the lights down at a set time each night, such as during scripture reading and prayers. Keep phones and tablets out of the bedroom. Sleep helps growing children learn, stay steady in their feelings, and stay well.
stages.9-11: Teach children why the lights go down at night so the habit becomes their own. Bedrooms should stay dark, without bright screens. Children this age are starting to manage their own routines, and the habits they form now often last.
stages.12-14: Teenagers' body clocks naturally shift later. Bright lights and screens late at night push their bedtime even later, so set a time for devices to leave the bedroom. Morning sunlight, such as a walk outside before school, helps them feel sleepy at a better hour.
stages.15-17: Help teens plan their own light: dim lamps and no glowing screens near bedtime, and bright daylight in the morning. A 2026 study found that late room light and short sleep make morning light less able to help a teen's body clock. Talk this through with your teen rather than only setting rules.
stages.18+: Young adults choose their own lights and screens. Their job is to keep evenings dim, mornings bright, and bedrooms dark, because rested people work, study, and serve better. Parents can share what they have learned and set a good example.

studies.finding: In preschool-age children, one hour of bright evening light cut the sleep hormone melatonin by about 88%. For 7 out of 10 children, the hormone had still not recovered 50 minutes after the light was turned off. This was a small study.
studies.source: Akacem et al., Physiological Reports (PMC), Sensitivity of the circadian system to evening bright light in preschool-age

studies.finding: In an NIH-funded study, preschoolers' melatonin dropped sharply at every light level tested before bedtime, even dim ones, and some children were more sensitive than others. This points to keeping light low and calm in the hour before a young child's bedtime.
studies.source: Hartstein et al., Journal of Pineal Research, reported by ScienceDaily (University of Colorado Boulder)

studies.finding: Bright morning light can help teenagers' body clocks shift earlier, so they can fall asleep at a better hour. But more room light late in the evening and less time to sleep made that morning light work less well. For teens, dim evenings and enough sleep go together with bright mornings.
studies.source: Scientific Reports (Nature Portfolio), Late evening room light and sleep restriction reduces the ability of bright morni

experts.say: Researchers who study child sleep found that young children are very sensitive to the effects of light at night, and some children more than others. Since homes now glow late into the evening, this is something to watch. The studies so far have been small, so the research is still early.
experts.who: Lauren Hartstein, PhD, Sleep and Development Lab, University of Colorado Boulder

experts.say: A researcher presenting early findings at a sleep science meeting said young children are sensitive to evening light and that the effect lasts after the light is turned off. She noted that this matters for how young children use electronic devices in the evening.
experts.who: Lameese Akacem, PhD, University of Colorado Boulder

experts.say: Scientists studying teenagers found that the good effect of bright morning light is weakened by late evening room light and short sleep. As evenings stay lit later, a family's habits of dim nights and bright mornings matter more.
experts.who: Study authors, Scientific Reports (Nature Portfolio)

future: Running your own light day: getting bright daylight in the morning, keeping evenings dim, and keeping the bedroom dark so sleep stays strong through school, work, and family life.
Setting up a home or workspace with good lighting: bright, clear light for reading and work, and soft, warm light for winding down.
Choosing when to turn off: knowing when to put away glowing screens and switch off lights to rest, think, and be with others.
Using electricity safely and wisely: handling lamps, cords, and switches safely, and not wasting power, so homes stay safe and costs stay low.
work: Light lets families and believers read the scriptures together and pray after the day's work is done, in every season of the year.
Hospitals and caregivers can care for the sick and injured through the whole night because of steady, safe light.
Churches, schools, and service groups can meet, teach, and help the poor in the evening, when working people are free to come.
A lit home in the evening gives families time to eat, talk, play, and grow close. Dimming it at bedtime protects the rest that children need.
ldsWork: Church leaders have taught that the Lord Himself is speeding up the use of technology to hasten temple and family history work. President Howard W. Hunter taught this, and Elder Quentin L. Cook repeated it in general conference (churchofjesuschrist.org/study/g

Elder Hamilton, who leads the Church's Family History Department, has taught that more records, better technology, and more temples are together hastening the Lord's work (thechurchnews.com/leaders/2025/03/10/elder-hamilton-on-how-rootstech-hastens-work-of-the

Leaders encourage members to use FamilySearch tools such as Ordinances Ready to find family names for the temple (thechurchnews.com/members/2024/12/15/ordinances-ready-familysearch-family-history-temple-work-elder-hamilton-alvarado/). Families can do this toge

bad: Hateful voices reaching millions at once.
Selling people things they do not need, all day long.
items.why: For the first time a sermon, a prophet, a hymn could reach every home at the same moment. General Conference, missionary broadcasts and the gospel in a hundred languages all ride on radio.

ages.16+: Curate what fills the house; it shapes everyone in it.
ages.3-5: Children's music and hymns; sing along.
ages.6-9: Audiobooks and scripture stories read aloud.
ages.10-12: Podcasts chosen together and listened to together first.
ages.13-15: Their music, checked against For the Strength of Youth by them, not only by you.

good: Music and stories for a family in the kitchen.
Warnings before a storm reaches you.
Good words reaching people who cannot read.
harm: Words and songs go in without a filter: explicit lyrics, adult talk, endless news.
kids: Ask who is talking and what they want.
Turn it off for dinner.
Sing along to the good stuff.
items.name: Radio
items.talk: If you had a radio show everyone in the world could hear, what would you say?
items.what: Voices and music sent through the air with no wire at all. One person speaks and a whole nation hears.
avoid: Music with explicit lyrics, even if the tune is good.
Talk shows and podcasts made for adults.
Radio or headphones on all day; silence is where thinking happens.
bless: Hymns and scripture audio in the car and the kitchen.
Make a family 'radio show' and send it to grandparents.
A playlist that lifts a friend who is down.
dangers: The first mass propaganda was on radio, and it helped start a world war.
A voice in the room feels like a friend even when it is not.

learned.note: Radio taught the world that a voice reaching millions must be chosen carefully. Every feed and channel since is the same lesson at a larger scale.

stages.0-2: Babies learn to talk by hearing your own voice and seeing your face. Gentle music or a hymn on the radio is fine for a short time if the sound is soft, but singing and talking with your baby matters far more than any broadcast, and the radio shouldn't play all day in the background.
stages.3-5: Let little ones listen with you to children's songs, stories and hymns, with the volume kept low. A family survey found that audio stories may help young children learn new words and come to love stories. Choose the station or program yourself, because young children can't yet sort good words from harmful ones.
stages.6-8: Children this age can enjoy radio stories, music and good programs with family, especially in the car, where you can talk about what you hear. Stay close by, because ads, news and song lyrics can be confusing or frightening at this age.
stages.9-11: Older children can start choosing some stations or programs themselves, using a short list you agree on, and practice turning off anything that feels wrong. Teach them that loud sound through headphones can harm hearing for good, so keep the volume low and take breaks.
stages.12-14: Young teens can listen more on their own, but keep talking with them about what lyrics, talk shows and ads are really saying, since they are working out who they are and are easily swayed by voices they admire. Agree together on safe headphone volume and on keeping devices out of bedrooms at night.
stages.15-17: Teens can manage their own listening, and you stay a trusted guide by asking what they enjoy and sharing what you love. Help them check news they hear against other trusted sources, and protect their hearing at concerts and on headphones.
stages.18+: Young adults choose for themselves. Radio and audio can be a source of news, learning, music and uplifting words, and a habit of listening carefully, checking facts and protecting their hearing will serve them all their lives.

studies.finding: In a 2026 survey of families with children under 5, parents said audio stories helped their children learn new words (40%) and grow an interest in stories and books (34.9%). These are parents' own reports, not a controlled trial, so this is early evidence.
studies.source: National Literacy Trust, 'Audiobooks and literacy' / 'Growing up listening: Audio stories in the early years' (with toni

studies.finding: About one billion young people worldwide could be at risk of hearing loss that cannot be undone, mostly from listening too loud for too long. WHO advises keeping the volume low, limiting how long you listen, and taking listening breaks.
studies.source: World Health Organization, Make Listening Safe

studies.finding: WHO and the International Telecommunication Union released a global safe-listening standard as part of WHO's Make Listening Safe work. It especially aims to improve listening habits among young people and is based on the latest evidence. The standard itself covers video games and esports, but the safe-listening habits apply to all audio.

Watching so much that there is no time left to live your own story.

ages.13-15: PG-13 with your judgment, never R; teach why, not just no.

Seeing places and people you could never visit.
Films that teach faith and courage.

Violence and sexual content seen young numb what should stay tender.
Long films replace play, sleep and talk.

If it makes you feel dark, turn it off.
Talk about the story afterwards.
items.name: Movies
items.talk: What is the best movie we have watched together, and what did it teach?
items.what: Pictures shown fast enough that they seem to move. A story you can watch with a crowd.
avoid: Ratings above their age, and PG-13 or R because 'everyone has seen it.'
Horror at any age of childhood.
Watching alone anything a parent has not seen.
bless: Family movie night with a film that lifts, then talk about it.
Make a family movie: a story, a play, a birthday, a farewell.
Watch the Savior's life together and talk about Him.
dangers: What you watch shapes what you want. Choose it like you choose friends.
Some films are made to frighten or excite in ways that stay with a child for years.

learned.note: Children copy what they see on screens more than what they are told. A parent watching beside them, asking 'was that right?', changes what the story teaches.

stages.0-2: Babies and toddlers learn best from real faces, hands and voices, so it is wisest to keep movies off at this age. Video calls with Grandma are fine.
stages.3-5: If you share a movie, pick a short, gentle one and watch it together. Young children can't yet tell what is pretend from what is real, so even a cartoon villain can feel real and scary.
stages.6-8: Family movies are fine in small amounts. Choose them ahead of time and keep scary or violent scenes out, because children this age often remember frightening pictures for a long time.
stages.9-11: Children can begin to help choose movies, using ratings and reviews together with you. Talk afterward about what was true, what was kind, and what the story wanted them to feel.
stages.12-14: Young teens want more freedom, and they can have it bit by bit. Keep agreed-upon limits on violent and sexual content, keep movies out of bedrooms at night, and keep watching some together, because the feeling and thinking parts of the brain are still growing.
stages.15-17: Teens can choose more on their own, guided by the standards your family has talked about. Help them notice how a film makes them feel, and protect their sleep from late-night watching.
stages.18+: Young adults choose for themselves. Movies can lift, teach and bring people together, and the best habit is to pick films that leave your heart better than you found it.

studies.finding: In a study of college students who remembered being frightened by a movie or TV show as children, about one in three said the fear lasted more than a year. Some had trouble sleeping or were afraid of certain places. Choosing calm, age-right films matters.
studies.source: Harrison & Cantor, 'Tales from the Screen: Enduring Fright Reactions to Scary Media,' Media Psychology

studies.finding: University of Michigan researchers followed up on that earlier study. They found that lasting fear and 'residual anxiety' can come not only from horror films but also from other disturbing scenes children saw growing up. Parents should look at every kind of content, not just scary movies.
studies.source: University of Michigan News

studies.finding: In one study of preschoolers, only 15% stayed within the American Academy of Pediatrics' limits for total screen time. About half (52%) did when only TV viewing was counted. Older preschoolers watched more. Simple family limits help, because most young children go over them.
studies.source: Journal of Clinical and Translational Science (abstract on PubMed Central)

experts.say: Joanne Cantor, who studies children and frightening media, reports that most people frightened by a program or movie as children felt it for a week or more. About a quarter still felt traces of that fear years later. Where scary films are easy to find, more children may carry fears like these.
experts.who: Joanne Cantor, PhD, Professor Emerita, University of Wisconsin–Madison
experts.source: Children's Fright Responses to Television and Films (Kids First / Coalition for Quality Children's Media)

experts.say: University of Michigan researchers found that long-lasting fear from childhood viewing can follow disturbing scenes of many kinds, not just horror films. Parents need to watch out for more than the 'scary movie' label.
experts.who: University of Michigan researchers

Shows that make wrong look normal.
Ads that teach children to want and want.

ages.16+: Decide what deserves an evening.

ages.10-12: Shows in the family room; learn what an ad is doing to you.
ages.13-15: Their own choices, measured against the family's standard.

good: Watching the prophet speak, as a family.
Learning about animals, places and history.
A game or a show that brings the family to one couch.

Hours of passive watching replace play, reading and sleep.
Advertising teaches a child to want.

items.name: Television
items.talk: What would our evenings look like with no TV for a week?
items.what: Movies and radio together, in a box in the living room. The world came into the house.
avoid: A television in a bedroom.
TV on during meals or as background all day.
Channels and streaming feeds that autoplay whatever comes next.
bless: Watch general conference and the Savior's story together.
Uplifting programs the whole family talks about afterwards.
Turn it off and read the story instead, some nights.
dangers: Hours a day in front of it are linked to less reading, less sleep and less play.
The living room stops being for talking.

learned.note: By the 1980s the average American child watched more television than they spent in school. It was the first screen to be blamed for what screens do, and the lessons learned then still hold.

stages.0-2: Keep the TV off for babies under about 18 months, except for video calls with family. Babies learn to talk by hearing your voice and watching your face, and a TV left on in the background means fewer words for them. From 18 months to 2 years, if you do watch, choose a short, gentle show and watch it together.
stages.3-5: Keep it to about one hour a day or less of good, slow-paced children's shows, and watch with your child so you can talk about what you see. Little ones learn best by playing, being read to, and moving, so TV should never crowd those out or cut into sleep.
stages.6-8: Set clear family rules for when and what to watch, keep TVs out of bedrooms, and turn the TV off at meals and before bed. Children this age believe what they see, so talk with them about stories, and explain that ads are made to sell things.
stages.9-11: Let your child help make a family media plan that says which shows, how long, and what comes first, like homework, chores, play, and sleep. Watch some shows together and ask good questions, such as 'What did that show want us to think?'
stages.12-14: Young teens want more choice, so agree together on what kinds of shows and how much is right, and check in often. This is a good age to practice turning it off on their own and noticing how shows and ads try to shape what they want and how they feel about themselves.
stages.15-17: Teens can choose more for themselves while you keep talking openly about what they watch and why. Help them guard sleep, school, friendships, and worship, and help them see that a good story can lift us while a poor one can drag us down.
stages.18+: Young adults make their own choices now. Encourage them to watch with purpose, keep the Sabbath and their sleep protected, and use good programs to learn, rest, and gather with people they love.

It says no screens before 18 months and about one hour a day of high-quality shows for ages 2 to 5. It also suggests a Family Media Plan and parents setting a good example.

studies.finding: A review of screen guidelines from around the world found that the World Health Organization recommends no screen time for babies under 1 and less than one hour a day for children ages 1 to 5, with less being better.
studies.source: Systematic review of screen-time recommendations, PubMed Central (summarizing WHO guidelines)

studies.finding: In a study that watched families at home, the longer a TV was on in the background, the less mothers talked with their babies and the less rich their talk was, even after accounting for family income and background.
studies.source: Journal of Child Language (Cambridge University Press), 'Infants' background television exposure and maternal language i

studies.finding: When a TV was on in the background, parents of 1- to 3-year-olds spoke fewer words and phrases to their children, including fewer new words, than when the TV was off.
studies.source: Journal of Children and Media, 'The Effects of Background Television on the Quantity and Quality of Child-Directed Speec

studies.finding: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends banning all commercial advertising to children younger than 7 and limiting ads aimed at older children and teens, because young children cannot yet tell when they are being sold to.
studies.source: American Academy of Pediatrics, 'Digital Advertising to Children' policy statement, Pediatrics

experts.say: Most screen platforms are built to keep people watching and to make money, not to help children grow. So families need help from the companies that design these products and from leaders, not just stricter rules at home.
experts.who: American Academy of Pediatrics, Council on Communications and Media
experts.source: HealthyChildren.org: A Child-Friendly Digital World: AAP Releases New Media Recommendations (2026)

experts.say: Screen time is like dessert: it is not bad in itself, but it is meant for small amounts. If a child or teen struggles to walk away from the screen, that is a sign of too much.
experts.who: Dr. Katherine Williamson, pediatrician, Rady Children's Mission Hospital
experts.source: CHOC Children's Health Hub: Updated AAP recommendations for screen time (2026)

experts.say: A TV left on in the background, even when no one is really watching, may quietly take away some of the talk babies need to learn language. Turning it off is a simple way to protect that time.
experts.who: Researchers in the Journal of Child Language
experts.source: Cambridge University Press, Journal of Child Language (home observation study)

experts.say: Advertising now reaches children in new and personal ways, including sponsored content, influencers, and ads shaped by data. Children need protection, and parents need to understand how these ads work.
experts.who: American Academy of Pediatrics
experts.source: Pediatrics: Digital Advertising to Children (policy statement)

future: Choosing on purpose: knowing what to watch, how long to watch, and when to turn it off, so shows serve your life instead of filling it.
Media literacy: telling news from opinion, story from advertising, and noticing when a program or ad is trying to change what you want or believe.
Learning from video: using good documentaries, lessons, and how-to programs to keep learning skills for school, work, and home all through life.
Telling stories well: understanding how video is made, so you can one day share good and true messages with others through it.

A family can watch a good program together and then talk about it, read scripture, and pray. That turns watching into a time of drawing closer to each other.
Broadcasts can bring worship services and words of comfort to people who are sick, elderly, or homebound, so they can still feel part of their church family.
Good documentaries and news help families learn about people in need near and far, so they can pray for them, give, and serve.
