bad: Cheating, stealing and spying, all made faster.
Machines built to keep people playing or scrolling.
items.why: Family history, scripture search, the app you are reading this in: all of it is a computer keeping track of what matters. It was built to think fast so that people could spend their thinking on what only people can do.

ages.16+: A tool for a life's work; they set the limits and keep them.
ages.3-5: Not needed.
ages.6-9: Learning games and typing, in a family room, with limits.
ages.10-12: Homework, coding for fun, a family history project; history visible to parents.
ages.13-15: Real work: writing, design, code, editing; filters stay on.

good: Finding your ancestors in records from around the world.
Helping doctors, farmers and teachers do more good.
Keeping the scriptures searchable in every language.
harm: Hours sitting still, hunched, staring.
A computer in a private room is a private door to the whole world.
kids: A computer is a tool, like a hammer. Use it to build.
Keep your passwords secret, even from friends.
When you are done, get up and go outside.
items.name: The Computer
items.talk: What is one thing a computer can never do that you can?
items.what: A machine that follows instructions, millions of times a second. It counts, sorts, remembers and draws.
avoid: A computer in a bedroom.
Accounts a parent does not know about.
Downloading what a parent has not approved.
bless: Learn to code and build something that helps someone.
Type up grandma's stories and the family's history.
Help index old records so families can find their ancestors.
dangers: What is stored on a computer can be stolen or lost.
A computer will do exactly what it is told, even when the instruction is wrong.

learned.note: The first computers filled rooms and were used to aim guns. Within a lifetime they were used to find grandmothers in old census books. Purpose is chosen, not built in.

stages.0-2: Babies and toddlers learn best by touching things, moving, and hearing loving voices face to face, so keep them away from computers and screens. Video calls with grandparents and family are a fine exception.
stages.3-5: If you use a computer at all, keep it to a little time each day (doctors suggest no more than about one hour) with good, slow, gentle programs, and sit beside your child and talk about what you see together. At this age, play, running, picture books and people do the most to grow a young mind and body.
stages.6-8: Children this age can start using a computer for short times to read, draw, and practice skills, in a shared family room where a parent is close by. Make sure screen time leaves plenty of room for sleep, outdoor play, chores and family time, because young bodies need to move.
stages.9-11: This is a good age to learn real skills like typing, searching carefully, and simple coding for school and creative projects. Keep the computer in a family room, take breaks to stretch and look far away or go outside, and talk often about what they find online.
stages.12-14: Young teens can do more on their own, but they need a family plan the whole family agrees on: what it is for, when, and where, with computers kept out of bedrooms at night. Their brains are still learning self-control, and many apps are built to keep them on longer, so they need you close and kind, not just rules.
stages.15-17: Teens can handle more of their own computer use for school, work and service, with your trust growing as they show good choices. Keep talking about sleep, honesty, kindness online, and noticing when it feels hard to walk away.
stages.18+: Young adults choose their own habits now, so help them keep a healthy balance of work, rest, movement and people. Encourage them to use the computer for learning, serving others and building a good life, and to set their own limits.

studies.finding: The American Academy of Pediatrics' newest guidance says most apps and platforms are built to keep children using them for profit, not to help them grow. It asks families to look at what children use and how it is designed, not only at how many minutes they spend. The guidance points out that well-made tools can help with learning and with staying close to others.
studies.source: American Academy of Pediatrics, policy statement 'Digital Ecosystems, Children, and Adolescents' (Pediatrics, February 2

studies.finding: Under the updated AAP guidance as a children's hospital explains it: no screens before 18 months, and about one hour a day of high-quality content for ages 2 to 5. The guidance cares more about quality, the setting, and talking together than about strict time limits.
studies.source: CHOC Children's Health Hub (Rady Children's Health)

studies.finding: A review that combined 45 studies covering more than 335,000 young people (average age about 9) found that each extra hour of screen time a day was linked to higher odds of nearsightedness, about 21% higher per hour. This shows the two go together, not that screens are proven to cause it. Breaks and outdoor time are a sensible response.
studies.source: JAMA Network Open, 'Digital Screen Time and Myopia: A Systematic Review and Dose-Response Meta-Analysis'

studies.finding: The World Health Organization says young children should not sit still for long stretches. For ages 2 to 4, sitting screen time should be no more than one hour a day, and less is better. Active play and good sleep matter most.
studies.source: World Health Organization, Guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep for children under 5 years of

studies.finding: The AAP says there is not yet enough evidence that one fixed screen-time limit helps every child, because children use screens for so many different things: schoolwork, reading, friends, hobbies and play. So the research is mixed, and what matters is the content and what screen time takes the place of.
studies.source: American Academy of Pediatrics, Center of Excellence on Social Media and Youth Mental Health, 'Screen Time Guidelines'

experts.say: When digital tools are built with children's wellbeing as the main goal, children can gain real good from them, like learning and friendship. The task is to make better tools and to support families.
experts.who: Dr. Tiffany Munzer, lead author of the AAP policy statement

experts.say: Pediatricians worry that as computers, phones and AI tools spread, many will keep being designed to hold children's attention for profit. They are asking the companies that make these products to build them in child-friendly ways.
experts.who: American Academy of Pediatrics, Council on Communications and Media

experts.say: Think of screen time like dessert: it is not bad in itself, but it should not crowd out the everyday things that help children grow. A warning sign is when a child struggles to walk away from the screen.
experts.who: Dr. Katherine Williamson, pediatrician, Rady Children's Mission Hospital

future: Typing, writing and organizing work on a computer: making documents, spreadsheets and presentations, the everyday tools of almost every job and calling.
Careful searching and thinking: finding good information, checking whether it is true, and knowing when a source or an AI answer might be wrong.
Basic coding and problem-solving: breaking a big problem into small steps, the way a computer follows instructions.
Self-control and safety online: protecting passwords and privacy, being kind and honest, and knowing when to step away and rest.
work: Computers help translate and print the Bible and share the message of Jesus Christ in many languages, so more people can read God's word in their own tongue.
They let families who live far apart see and talk to each other, pray together, and stay close.
Hospitals, doctors and charities use computers to care for the sick, keep track of who needs help, and get food and supplies to the poor faster.
Children and parents can use them to study scriptures, learn hymns, and find good lessons that build faith at home.
ldsWork: Through FamilySearch, the Church's free family history website, families use computers to find their ancestors, build family trees, and prepare names so sacred temple ordinances can be done for them.
Volunteers around the world use computers to help make old records searchable, so more families can be joined together through temple work.

Church leaders have taught that we can use technology to share the restored gospel of Jesus Christ and to help gather Israel on both sides of the veil, which helps prepare the world for the Savior's Second Coming.

bad: Games built to keep you playing and spending, with no end.
Games where hurting people is the fun part.
Strangers in a game chat who are not who they say.
items.why: Play is how children learn. A good game teaches patience, problem-solving and teamwork, and a family that plays together laughs together. Games can be built to teach anything, including scripture.

ages.16+: Their own hours, but the same rule: real people before pixels.
ages.3-5: None, or a few minutes of a simple touch game on a parent's lap.
ages.6-9: E-rated games, together, with a timer everyone can see.
ages.10-12: E10+ games, no online chat, a timer, and weekends more than school nights.
ages.13-15: T-rated with a parent's judgment; chat only with known friends; no loot boxes; no games in bedrooms.

good: Playing together as a family and laughing.
Games that teach maths, reading, music or the scriptures.
Making your own game and learning how things work.
harm: Games are built to keep a child playing: rewards, streaks and loot boxes work on a young brain like slot machines.
Violence rehearsed for hours teaches the hands and dulls the heart.
Chat and voice with strangers; predators go where children play.
kids: Play with people you know.
Set a timer before you start, and stop when it rings.
Never buy anything in a game without asking.
items.name: Video Games
items.talk: What game could we play together this week, and what does it teach?
items.what: A game you play on a screen. Pong, then Mario, then whole worlds.
avoid: Games rated above their age (E is for everyone; T is for teens; M is not for children).
Online chat or voice with anyone the family does not know in person.
Loot boxes and in-game purchases; that is gambling with a costume on.
Playing in a bedroom, or after bedtime.
bless: Play together as a family; a game can be a table everyone sits at.
Creative games: build a temple, a city, a world, and show it off.
Invite a lonely child to play in the same room.
dangers: Some games are designed like slot machines; the 'loot box' is a bet.
Hours disappear; sleep, homework and friends disappear with them.
Online chat inside games is where strangers reach children most.

learned.note: Several countries now treat loot boxes as gambling and limit game time for children. Games with a clear end and games played beside a parent show none of the harms of endless online ones.
A systematic review found that excessive video game play is associated with poorer academic performance and increased behavioral problems in children.
A review by Johns Hopkins Children's Center found that specially designed video games can modestly improve mental health in children and teens with anxiety, depression, and ADHD.

A global study involving over 2.8 million children across 64 countries found that increased screen time, including video games, is linked to poorer academic achievement and language development, as well as higher socioemotional and mental health problems.

A systematic review and meta-analysis revealed that exergaming can promote physical activity and improve cognitive flexibility in children, though its effects on motor skills and other cognitive functions were not statistically significant.

A study of preschool children found that brief digital or traditional gameplay improved performance on tasks requiring quick responses but reduced performance on tasks demanding greater concentration and self-control.

A systematic review and meta-analysis indicated that exergaming has significant effects on glucose and lipid metabolism in children and adolescents, suggesting potential benefits for managing metabolic health.

A scoping review found that video and app-based games could serve as beneficial tools to support youth emotion regulation through various strategies, though some studies reported areas of continued difficulty.

stages.0-2: Babies and toddlers should not play video games. They learn best by touching real things, hearing loving voices, and moving their bodies, and the World Health Organization advises no screen time for babies under 1 and very little for children under 2.
stages.3-5: If a young child plays at all, keep it short (under an hour a day, and less is better), choose slow, gentle games made for small children, and play beside them. Children this age grow through running, pretend play, sleep, and talking with you, so a game should never take the place of those.
stages.6-8: Short, planned game time in a shared room can be fine, with games rated for young children, voice and text chat turned off, and no in-game spending. At this age children are still learning to stop doing something fun, so a parent sets the timer and helps them turn the game off.
stages.9-11: Children this age can enjoy building, puzzle and team games, and some research links regular gaming to better attention and memory, but keep clear limits, avoid loot boxes and other paid 'mystery prizes', and keep chat with strangers off. They are starting to want friends' approval and can be talked into things, so talk often about who they meet in games and what to do if someone makes them uneasy
stages.12-14: Young teens can take on more freedom, with family rules about time, ratings, spending and age-checked chat, and with screens kept out of bedrooms at night. Their brains are still learning to put the brakes on, so watch for gaming that pushes out sleep, schoolwork, friends or faith, and step in kindly if it does.
stages.15-17: Older teens can mostly manage their own gaming while practising balance, and parents should stay close enough to talk. Help them notice how games are built to keep them playing, and how 'loot boxes' and betting on game items are close to gambling, so they learn to choose for themselves.
stages.18+: Young adults choose for themselves. They can enjoy games as rest, friendship or even a career in making games, while keeping them in their place beside work, study, service, family and worship. If gaming starts to take over their life and they can't stop, it is wise and brave to seek help.

studies.finding: In nearly 2,000 children aged 9 to 10 in the large U.S. ABCD study, those who played video games 3 or more hours a day did a little better on tests of attention and memory and showed different brain activity than children who never played. The study shows a link, not proof that games cause the gains, and it did not look at sleep, mood or other trade-offs.
studies.source: Chaarani et al., JAMA Network Open (ABCD study), reported by PsyPost

studies.finding: A 2025 review of the research found a clear link between children and teens using loot boxes and gambling behaviour, and warned that loot boxes may act as a 'gateway' to gambling. Most of these studies show a link rather than proving that one causes the other.
studies.source: Trends in Psychiatry and Psychotherapy (review)

studies.finding: A study that followed adolescents over time, published in International Gambling Studies, found that those who played games with gambling-like features such as loot boxes were more likely to gamble with real money later.
studies.source: Science Media Centre Spain, reporting on International Gambling Studies

studies.finding: The World Health Organization advises no screen time for babies under 1, and no more than one hour a day of sitting screen time for children aged 2 to 4 (less is better), with active play, reading and sleep in its place.
studies.source: World Health Organization

experts.say: Gaming may help children's attention, memory and visual skills, but researchers say they need to follow these children over time to know whether the effects last and whether games actually cause them.
experts.who: Bader Chaarani, University of Vermont, ABCD study co-investigator

experts.say: As games mix in more gambling-like features such as loot boxes, more young people may move from these features to real-money gambling. Researchers are calling for stronger age limits and better game rules.
experts.who: Researchers reviewing loot box studies in youth

experts.say: Big game platforms are starting to require age checks before players can chat, and to limit chat to people of similar ages. The aim is to make it harder for adults to contact children they don't know, but parents' settings and watchful care still matter.
experts.who: Roblox

future: Self-control with screens: being able to stop a game, see the hooks built in to keep you playing, and choose sleep, people and duty first.
Working as a team online: talking clearly, sharing a plan and being kind with people you are working with far away, as many jobs now need.
Making, not just playing: building game worlds, coding, design and simulation, skills used in engineering, medicine, training and the arts.
Staying safe and wise with money online: knowing what in-game spending and 'mystery prizes' really cost, and guarding your privacy from strangers.
work: Games and simple story apps can help children learn Bible stories and verses in many languages, in a way they enjoy.
Playing together can bring a family closer: parents and children laughing, solving problems and taking turns side by side.
Doctors use games and game-style tools to help sick children through hard treatments and to help people heal after injury.
Game-making skills can be used to build tools for learning, for charities and for reaching people with the message of Jesus Christ in their own language.
ldsWork: Church leaders have taught that technology is given to help the Lord's work move faster, including sharing the restored gospel. The skills young people learn in games, such as patience, teamwork and building things, can be turned to that service.
FamilySearch has used game-style tools such as badges, goals and simple challenges to help youth and families find their ancestors. That helps prepare names for temple ordinances.

Leaders have also warned that the same tools can waste time and push out what matters most. Families can set limits so that gaming never crowds out prayer, scripture study, temple worship or ministering, which help prepare the world for the Savior.

bad: Sitting alone in a room for hours.
Copying other people's work and calling it yours.
items.why: Family history left the archives and came home. A parent could type the family's stories, print a lesson, and keep the records Heavenly Father asked us to keep, in the kitchen.

ages.16+: Their own workstation, their own standards.
ages.3-5: Not needed.
ages.6-9: A family computer in a family room, with a child account.
ages.10-12: Homework and creating; a parent can see everything.
ages.13-15: Real tools, with the filter still on and the door open.

good: Writing the family's history and printing it for the grandchildren.
Learning any skill from your own desk.
Running a small business from home.
harm: The whole world on a desk, good and bad alike, unless a parent shapes it.
kids: Use it where the family can see the screen.
Save your work, then save it again.
Make something with it, not just watch something on it.
items.name: The Personal Computer
items.talk: What could you create on a computer that would bless somebody?
items.what: A computer small and cheap enough to sit on a family's desk.
avoid: A home computer without a filter and a family account.
Private browsing and cleared history.
Free downloads that carry viruses and worse.
bless: Write a book, design a card, make music, edit a family film.
Learn a skill that will one day feed a family.
Help an elderly neighbor with their computer.
dangers: A computer in a child's bedroom is a door with no one watching it.
Files can be lost in a second; keep a copy.

learned.note: The rule that came out of the personal computer years still works best: keep it in a shared room where the screen faces the family.

stages.0-2: Keep babies away from the computer, except for video calls with Grandma or a parent who is away. Little ones learn best from real faces, voices, and hands-on play. If you start some screen use between 18 and 24 months, choose good programs and sit with your child.
stages.3-5: Keep computer time short, about an hour a day or less, and choose gentle, good-quality programs. Sit and use it together. Young children learn best by playing and talking with people, so the computer should not replace either one.
stages.6-8: Let children use the computer for learning, making things, and family projects. Keep it in a shared room where a parent is close by. Set clear time limits so there is still time for sleep, play outside, reading, and family.
stages.9-11: Use your family media plan to teach children to search carefully, protect their privacy, and come tell you when they see something bad online. Keep the computer out of the bedroom and turn screens off an hour before bed. At this age children are learning to make their own choices, and they still need you guiding them.
stages.12-14: Give teens a little more freedom as they show they can be trusted, and keep talking with them about what they see and who they meet online. Studies on social media and teen mental health are mixed. Still, the U.S. Surgeon General has said it is not yet shown to be safe enough for young people, so go slowly and stay close.
stages.15-17: Help teens use the computer for real work like writing, coding, making things, and getting ready for a job. Let them help set the family's rules for screen-free time and sleep. Their judgment is still growing, so you are now more of a coach and a safe place to come to.
stages.18+: Young adults choose for themselves now. Encourage them to make the computer a tool for work, learning, and serving others, and not something that runs their days. Show them by how you use your own computer that it can be put away for rest, worship, and people.

studies.finding: In its first big update in ten years, the American Academy of Pediatrics no longer gives one screen-time number for every child. It asks families to look at the quality of what children use, what screen time pushes aside, and how the family uses media together. It suggests a Family Media Plan, screen-free time for sleep, play, reading, and family, and no devices in bedrooms.
studies.source: American Academy of Pediatrics, 'Digital Ecosystems, Children, and Adolescents' policy statement, Pediatrics

studies.finding: For families who want a number, the AAP says limits might be under one hour a day for toddlers and preschoolers. For school-age children and teens, it suggests one to two hours or more of entertainment (not schoolwork). It also advises no screens in the hour before bed.
studies.source: American Academy of Pediatrics, Pediatrics policy statement

studies.finding: Around the world, students who used digital devices for learning at school for up to about an hour a day did better in math than students who used none. More than an hour was linked to lower scores, and about 3 in 10 students said devices distracted them. These findings show patterns, not proof of cause and effect.
studies.source: OECD, PISA 2022 Results

studies.finding: Child psychiatrists advise that babies under 18 months use screens only for video chats with an adult. Between 18 and 24 months, they suggest only educational programs watched with a caregiver. They also say not to use screens as a babysitter or to stop tantrums, and to talk with children about what they see.
studies.source: American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, Screen Time and Children

experts.say: Social media can bring some young people real benefits. But children are often shown extreme or harmful content, and we cannot yet say it is safe enough for children and teens.
experts.who: Dr. Vivek Murthy, then U.S. Surgeon General
experts.source: Social Media and Youth Mental Health: The U.S. Surgeon General's Advisory (2023)

experts.say: The question is less how to limit screen time and more how a family uses screens together. Shared meals without devices help children grow healthy and close to others.
experts.who: Pediatric expert interviewed about the AAP's 2026 guidance

experts.say: Using computers for learning in moderation goes with better results, but heavy use and distraction go with worse results. Strict device bans in class may also stop students from learning to manage devices themselves.
experts.who: OECD education researchers (PISA)

experts.say: Employers expect AI and big data, networks and cybersecurity, and technological literacy to be the fastest-growing skills between now and 2030.
experts.who: World Economic Forum

future: Technological literacy: using a computer with confidence to write, calculate, organize, and learn new programs as they change.
Staying safe online: protecting passwords, privacy, and personal information, the everyday basics of cybersecurity.
Finding good information: searching carefully, checking whether a source can be trusted, and using AI tools wisely and honestly.
Self-control with screens: knowing when to put the computer away so it serves your work, rest, and relationships.
work: Families can read and study the Bible together on a computer, in many languages and translations, and look up helps that make the stories clear.
Believers can share messages of Jesus Christ's love with friends and neighbors near and far, kindly and truthfully.
Churches and families can use computers to organize meals, rides, and visits for people who are sick, lonely, or in need, and to give to trusted charities.
Families far apart can see and hear each other on video calls, so grandparents, missionaries, and children stay close.
ldsWork: FamilySearch, a free online tool, helps members find their ancestors, see which temple ordinances still need to be done, and prepare those names for the temple (churchofjesuschrist.org, Introduction to Family History, ch. 7: https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org

Church leaders have said FamilySearch is meant to be so easy that even children can do family history, which helps families join together across generations (Church News, 2025: https://www.thechurchnews.com/leaders/2025/03/10/what-church-leaders-wish-members-u

Elder David A. Bednar invited members to use technology to 'sweep the earth as with a flood' with messages of righteousness and truth. He also warned that misused technology can waste time and harm relationships (churchofjesuschrist.org: https://www.churchofje

bad: Pornography reached homes through this door, and it reaches children first.
Lies that spread around the world before the truth has its shoes on.
Strangers who pretend to be friends.
items.why: The gospel to every nation, kindred, tongue and people: the internet is the road that promise travels on. Scriptures in a hundred languages, family history from every country, a prophet's words the moment they are spoken.

ages.16+: Their own filters and habits, built while you were still there to help.
ages.3-5: No browsing; a parent plays the chosen video.
ages.6-9: Filtered, in a family room, on a short list of sites you chose, with a parent beside them.
ages.10-12: Filtered and monitored in family rooms; teach the plan for a bad page: close it, tell a parent, never punished.
ages.13-15: Filters plus accountability; talk often about what they meet; they know you will ask.

good: Scriptures, talks and family records for the whole world, free.
Learning anything from anyone, anywhere.
Finding your family across oceans.
harm: Pornography finds children before they look for it: most first see it by accident, around age twelve, and it teaches lies about love and bodies.
Predators, scams and bullying reach into a bedroom.
Endless information with no way to tell true from false.
kids: If you see something yucky, look away and tell a grown-up. You are not in trouble.
Never tell a stranger where you live or go to school.
Ask before you download anything.
items.name: The Internet and the Web
items.talk: What is the best thing the internet has brought into our home? What is the worst?
items.what: Every computer in the world able to talk to every other one. The web put pages on it that anyone can read.
work: The scriptures and the good news of Jesus Christ can now be read and heard for free, in many languages, by people almost anywhere in the world.
Families far apart can pray, talk and see each other by video, which keeps love strong across miles.
People who serve the poor and the sick can share needs, gather help and send aid quickly when disaster strikes.
Good music, uplifting talks and kind messages can reach someone who is lonely or searching, right when they need it.
avoid: Unfiltered browsing anywhere, on any device, including a friend's.
Searching alone before they know what to do with what appears.
Clicking ads, pop-ups and 'free' downloads.
Private browsing modes and cleared histories.
bless: Learn anything: a language, an instrument, how to fix the sink.
Find a scripture, a talk, a hymn in seconds and share it.
Serve: find who needs help, and organize the helpers.
future: Telling true from false: checking who wrote something, comparing sources, and spotting fake pictures, AI-made content and scams.
Searching and learning well: finding good information fast, and using online courses and tools to keep learning for life.
Working with people online: writing kind, clear messages, sharing files and working on teams by video and chat.
Staying safe and in charge: protecting passwords and privacy, and choosing when to put the screen down so the tool serves you and doesn't rule you.

stages.0-2: Babies and toddlers learn by touching, moving and hearing a loving voice. The World Health Organization advises no screens before age one and very little after that, so keep the internet for short video calls with grandparents while you hold your child.
stages.18+: Young adults will use the internet for work, school, faith and friendship every day. Help them keep healthy habits they choose for themselves: a plan for their own time, care about what is true, and turning away from what harms the spirit.
stages.3-5: Young children can't yet tell a real thing from an ad, or a safe page from a scary one. Use the internet together for less than an hour a day, on a shared device in a family room, and choose good shows and calls with family.
stages.6-8: Children this age are learning to read and ask big questions, and they trust whatever they see. Let them explore a few chosen sites or apps on a shared family tablet with parental controls on, and teach them one rule: if anything makes you feel bad or confused, tell me, and you won't be in trouble.
stages.9-11: Children now do schoolwork online and want more freedom, but the parts of the brain that slow us down and keep us safe are still growing. Keep devices out of bedrooms at night, keep filters on, and talk calmly about pornography and strangers before they run into them. Most children first see pornography by accident, around age twelve.
stages.12-14: Early teens care deeply about friends and fitting in, so mean comments, scams and pressure can hurt them more. Make a family media plan together, wait on social media, check in often about what they see, and keep phones charging outside the bedroom.
stages.15-17: Teens are practising for adult life and need room to make choices, with a parent still close by. Slowly give them more trust as they show good judgment, keep talking about what's true online and what love really is, and protect their sleep.

dangers: The average child first sees pornography online around age 12, often by accident.
Everything posted can be copied and kept forever.
A screen with no limits is a river with no banks.

experts.say: The AAP says to think about more than minutes on a screen. Parents can ask what the child is watching, whether they use it to calm down, and what it 'crowds out', like sleep, play and family time.
experts.who: American Academy of Pediatrics, Council on Communications and Media
experts.source: AAP News, 'Beyond screen time: Policy discusses how to approach immersive digital ecosystem'

experts.say: As AI tools spread online, more children are coming across fake, computer-made sexual images, mostly without looking for them. This makes it even more important for parents to start the conversation early.
experts.who: Common Sense Media researchers
experts.source: Teens in the AI Era: Pornography and Sexual Content (2026)

experts.say: Some good news: pediatricians and tech companies are starting to work together. The AAP's Family Media Plan helped shape new parental controls, so families have easier tools to balance screens with sleep, exercise, schoolwork and time together.
experts.who: American Academy of Pediatrics
experts.source: AAP News, 'AAP, Apple release guide to help build healthy digital habits'

experts.say: The Surgeon General asked lawmakers and companies, not only parents, to make online spaces safer for children, because families shouldn't have to carry this alone.
experts.who: U.S. Surgeon General
experts.source: Social Media and Youth Mental Health advisory

ldsWork: Through FamilySearch, a free service of the Church, members can find their ancestors in records from around the world and prepare their names for temple ordinances. Church leaders have taught that this is part of gathering Israel on both sides of the veil.
The Gospel Library app and churchofjesuschrist.org put the scriptures, general conference talks and Come, Follow Me lessons in many languages, helping families learn of the Savior at home.

Church leaders, including Elder David A. Bednar in 'To Sweep the Earth as with a Flood', have invited members to use the internet and social media to share uplifting messages about Jesus Christ, helping prepare the world for His Second Coming.

learned.note: Filters and family rules help, but the thing that works most is a parent who talks about it early and often, before something is seen, not after.

A study in the Journal of Development Economics found that early exposure to high-speed internet may negatively impact children's communication and social skills, highlighting the need for mindful internet use.

studies.source: American Academy of Pediatrics, 'Digital Ecosystems, Children, and Adolescents' policy statement, Pediatrics
studies.finding: The American Academy of Pediatrics no longer gives one screen-time number for every child. It asks families to make a Family Media Plan together, set parental controls, keep screen-free family time, keep devices out of bedrooms, and stop screens an hour before bed. As a rough guide, it suggests under an hour a day for toddlers and preschoolers and about one to two hours of fun (not school) screen

studies.source: Common Sense Media, 'Teens in the AI Era: Pornography and Sexual Content'
studies.finding: 74% of U.S. teens say they have seen online pornography, and 52% saw it by age 12, often by accident. 44% have seen AI-made sexual content. This is a survey, so it shows how common this is but doesn't prove what causes it. It is a strong reason to talk with children early and calmly.

studies.source: World Health Organization guidelines, as reported by the American Optometric Association
studies.finding: For children under five, the World Health Organization advises no screen time under age one and no more than one hour a day for ages two to four, and less is better. It wants that time spent on active play, sleep, and reading and talking together.

studies.source: U.S. Surgeon General's Advisory on Social Media and Youth Mental Health (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services)
studies.finding: The U.S. Surgeon General's advisory found that we can't yet say social media is safe enough for children and teens, and it urged families and companies to act now. The research is still growing and the findings are mixed: the internet helps some young people connect, while others are harmed.

bad: Texting while driving.
Being with people but not really with them.
items.why: A mother can be called from anywhere. Help can be summoned from a roadside. Missionaries in far places can reach their families. The phone in a pocket was made to keep people safe and close.

ages.0-2: A parent's phone is not a pacifier.
ages.16+: Their phone, with limits they wrote and keep.
ages.3-5: Still not a toy; video calls with family only.
ages.6-9: No phone of their own.
ages.10-12: A basic phone or watch that calls and texts, only if the family truly needs it.
ages.13-15: A smartphone only with a written family agreement, filters, and no bedroom overnight; many families wait until high school.

good: Calling for help wherever you are.
Telling your family you are safe.
A quick 'I love you' in the middle of a day.
harm: A phone that is always there is always pulling.
Texts at night steal sleep; texts from strangers steal safety.
kids: Phones down at the table.
Never text a driver, and never text while riding a bike.
Answer your parents.
items.name: The Mobile Phone
items.talk: When is a phone a helper, and when is it a wall between us?
items.what: A telephone with no wire, small enough to carry. Anyone could be reached anywhere.
work: Scriptures in your pocket: the Bible and other holy books can be read and heard on a phone in many languages, so people almost anywhere can learn about Jesus Christ.
Staying close as a family: calls, texts and video chats help parents, children and grandparents far apart pray together, share news and lift each other up.
Serving others: a quick call or message lets us check on a lonely neighbor, plan meals for a sick friend, or call for help in an emergency.
Sharing good news gently: a kind message, a verse of scripture or an invitation to church can reach a friend at just the right moment.
avoid: A phone in the bedroom overnight.
Group chats a parent does not know about.
A phone at the table or in the car with the driver.
bless: A text that says 'I'm praying for you' at the right moment.
Call the person, not just the text.
Coordinate service: rides, meals, visits.
future: Self-control with a phone: choosing when to put it away, turning off alerts, and protecting sleep, prayer, study and time with people.
Clear, kind and careful communication: writing messages, emails and calls that are polite, honest and right for work, school and family.
Staying safe online: spotting scams and strangers, keeping private information private, using strong passwords, and knowing when to ask for help.
Using a phone as a tool for learning and work: finding true information, managing a calendar, using maps, banking and work apps, and checking whether a source can be trusted.

stages.0-2: Babies and toddlers should not have their own phone. They learn by looking at faces, hearing voices and playing with real things. A short video call with a grandparent while you hold them is a good use, and it is best when you stay close and talk with them about who they see.
stages.18+: Young adults choose for themselves now. Parents can still show by example and talk openly about using the phone to learn, work, serve and stay close to family, without letting it rule their time, sleep or peace.
stages.3-5: Young children still do not need a phone of their own. If they use yours, keep it short, sit with them, and use it for good things like calling family. They grow best through play, talk, sleep and time outdoors.
stages.6-8: Children this age do not need their own phone yet. Teach them how to call you or 911 on a family phone in an emergency, and tell them never to answer messages from people they do not know. They are learning right from wrong and still need a grown-up close by.
stages.9-11: Many families choose to wait. Some give a simple phone that only calls and texts, or a watch phone, so a child can reach home. In one large 2025 study, the younger children were when they got a smartphone, the more likely they were to be short on sleep and overweight by age 12. So keep phones out of the bedroom at night and make rules together.
stages.12-14: If you give a smartphone at this age, give it slowly and stay close. Start with a few apps, keep it in shared rooms, put it outside the bedroom at night, and keep talking. Young teens feel friends' opinions strongly and are still learning to stop themselves, so they need a parent's steady help.
stages.15-17: Teens can carry more of the load: making their own plan for school, sleep, church and family time, with parents checking in instead of watching every step. Keep the phone out of the bedroom overnight, because teens need 8 to 10 hours of sleep and late-night phone use often cuts into it.

dangers: Distracted driving kills thousands a year; a text can wait.
A phone that is always on you means work and worry are always on you too.

experts.say: As almost every child gets a phone by early high school, children's health can be affected even when their use does not look like a 'problem.' The researchers are not asking for bans. They want more research on the best age to get a phone, what kind of phone, and what it is used for.
experts.who: Authors of the 2025 Pediatrics smartphone study

experts.say: Many children use their phones between midnight and 5 a.m. on school nights. Getting devices physically out of the bedroom at bedtime may be the single most important screen rule for protecting sleep.
experts.who: Jean Twenge, psychologist, San Diego State University
experts.source: Institute for Family Studies (excerpt from '10 Rules for Raising Kids in a High-Tech World', 2025)

experts.say: School phone bans alone may not improve children's mental health if their phone use outside school stays the same. Even so, bans may still help students focus and take part in school.
experts.who: Helen Weiss and Chris Bonell, London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine

experts.say: Phones may bring real benefits to children's wellbeing, but public posting and phones in bed bring risks. Long-term research that follows children over many years is needed to learn how to keep the good and reduce the harm.
experts.who: Chighaf Bakour and colleagues, University of South Florida College of Public Health

ldsWork: Family history in your hand: with the free FamilySearch Tree and Memories apps, families can find ancestors, add photos and stories, and prepare names for temple ordinances anywhere (familysearch.org).

Gospel Library: the Gospel Library app puts the scriptures, Come, Follow Me and general conference messages in many languages on a phone, so families can study together at home (churchofjesuschrist.org).

Helping gather Israel on both sides of the veil: President Russell M. Nelson taught that the gathering of Israel is the most important work on earth. Phones help members share the gospel with friends and do family history and temple work for those who have die

learned.note: The mobile phone taught families the phrase 'phones down at dinner'. It is still the single best rule.

Research in BMC Public Health showed that increased screen use in early childhood is associated with shorter sleep duration and more sleep problems, emphasizing the importance of managing screen time.
Research suggests that excessive smartphone use can negatively impact adolescents' cognitive development, leading to decreased attention spans and academic performance.

A study in the U.S. linked excessive screen time in children and adolescents to higher risks of anxiety, depression, behavior problems, and ADHD, with physical activity and sleep as mediating factors.
A meta-analysis revealed that parental device use during parent-child interactions is moderately to largely associated with children's internalizing and externalizing mental health problems.
A systematic review indicated that excessive screen use negatively impacts sleep duration and quality in preschool children, potentially leading to behavioral and cognitive issues.
A meta-analysis found that digital interventions can effectively promote mental health in children and adolescents, suggesting potential benefits of technology when used appropriately.
A recent study found that children who use mobile devices at bedtime are more likely to experience reduced sleep quality and duration, leading to increased daytime sleepiness.
Experts recommend keeping phones and tablets out of children's bedrooms overnight to prevent disrupted sleep and compulsive use.
A study found that excessive screen time in children is associated with mental health issues and ADHD, mediated by reduced physical activity and irregular sleep patterns.

studies.source: Pediatrics (American Academy of Pediatrics), reported in AAP News
studies.finding: In a large U.S. study, 12-year-olds who owned a smartphone had about 30% higher odds of depression, 40% higher odds of obesity and 60% higher odds of not getting enough sleep than children without one. Children who got phones younger had higher odds of poor sleep and obesity. The study could not prove the phone caused these problems, and the authors said phones need 'dedicated oversight' rather th

studies.source: Peer-reviewed study on parental evening screen rules and teen sleep (PubMed Central)
studies.finding: Teens whose parents made them leave their phones outside the bedroom at night slept about 33 minutes longer on average. Only this strict rule, keeping the phone out of the room, was clearly linked to more sleep.

studies.source: The Lancet Regional Health – Europe (Goodyear et al., SMART Schools), with commentary by Weiss and Bonell
studies.finding: A study of about 1,200 students aged 12 to 15 in 30 UK schools found that phone bans during the school day were not linked to better mental wellbeing, sleep or grades, because students did not use their phones less overall. Experts said phone use at home and in the evening may matter more. Other researchers have questioned this study's methods, so the research is still mixed.

studies.source: University of South Florida College of Public Health
studies.finding: A University of South Florida survey found that children with their own smartphones did better than those without on most of the wellbeing measures it looked at, while posting publicly on social media was linked to harm. One in four children slept with a phone in their hand or bed, and they got less sleep than children whose phones stayed in another room (8.6 vs. 9.3 hours). This shows the researc

studies.source: Pediatrics (American Academy of Pediatrics), 'The Family Media Plan'
studies.finding: The American Academy of Pediatrics offers a free Family Media Plan. It helps families choose their own rules, such as screen-free places in the home, where phones go at night, and protecting sleep and at least one hour of physical activity each day.

bad: Comparing your real life to everyone else's best moments.
Bullying that follows a child home and into bed.
Feeds built to keep you scrolling long after you wanted to stop.
items.why: At its best it is the ward newsletter for the whole world: families far apart share a birthday, a missionary shares the gospel, a lonely person finds a friend. The good in it is real, and it is why so many wanted it.

ages.16+: Purposeful use with their own limits; a weekly day away from it.
ages.3-5: None.
ages.6-9: None.
ages.10-12: None; the law says 13 and the Surgeon General says even that is not proof of safety.
ages.13-15: Delay it as long as you can. If it is used: private accounts, parents follow and know the passwords, notifications off, a daily limit, nothing in bedrooms.

good: Keeping in touch with family who live far away.
Sharing something good and true with many people at once.
Finding others who believe what you believe.
harm: Built to keep a child scrolling: the feed never ends, and every like is a small reward on a young brain.
Comparison, exclusion, bullying and sextortion happen here; teens who use it three or more hours a day face double the risk of anxiety and depression symptoms (U.S. Surgeon General, 2023).
Sleep loss, and a self-worth that rises and falls with strangers' approval.
kids: No account until you are old enough, and your parents say when.
Never post something you would not want Grandma to see.
If someone is mean to you online, show a grown-up right away.
items.name: Social Media
items.talk: We saw what social media did to a lot of kids before anyone knew. What would you want to know before you got an account?
items.what: Websites and apps where everyone posts and everyone watches. Facebook, then Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat and the rest.
work: Sharing the good news of Jesus Christ: a short verse, a hymn or a testimony can reach friends and strangers in many lands in a single day.
Bringing the scriptures and uplifting messages to people in their own language, wherever they live.
Gathering help for the poor, the sick and people hit by disasters: families can find out who needs meals, rides or prayers, and answer quickly.
Strengthening families: grandparents, missionaries and cousins far away can share pictures, birthdays and faith, so love stays close even across oceans.
avoid: Any account under 13 (that is the law) and, most experts now say, well after.
Secret accounts, second accounts, and direct messages with strangers.
Posting photos of their body, their school, their home or their location.
Endless scrolling; use it for a purpose and put it down.
bless: Share a testimony, a scripture, a kindness, on purpose.
Organize a service project with friends.
Keep a family group where the good news gets told first.
future: Self-control with screens: choosing when to log on and when to put the phone down, so that an app doesn't decide for you.
Telling true from false: checking where a post came from before believing it or sharing it.
Kind, wise speaking online: writing in a way that builds people up, guarding your privacy, and remembering that what you post can stay online for years.
Sharing good work with others: many jobs, businesses and service groups now use social media to tell people about their work and find people to help.

stages.0-2: No social media at all. Babies and toddlers learn by looking at real faces, hearing real voices and playing with their hands, so a video call with Grandma is fine, but scrolling feeds are not.
stages.18+: Young adults choose for themselves. Help them choose on purpose: limit what pulls them away from God, sleep and people, follow what feeds their soul, and use their voice to share light and truth.
stages.3-5: No social media. Young children can't yet tell a show from an ad or a stranger from a friend, so keep screens few, choose good ones, watch them together, and let video calls with family be the 'social' part.
stages.6-8: No accounts of their own yet. Children this age are learning to read, make friends and handle feelings face to face. A parent can show them a family photo or a Church video and talk about it together.
stages.9-11: Still no accounts of their own. Most big apps say users must be at least 13, and children this age are very tender about fitting in. Use these years to make a family media plan and to practice kindness and saying 'no' when something online feels wrong.
stages.12-14: Wait as long as you can. If you do start, go slowly with one app, private settings, phones out of bedrooms at night, and set times to check instead of scrolling whenever bored. Young teens' brains are wired to want approval from friends, so talk often about what they see and how it makes them feel.
stages.15-17: Teens can be given more freedom step by step, while the family plan still guards sleep, schoolwork, church, chores and real-life friends. Older teens are growing toward running their own lives, so coach them more than you police them, and help them post things that lift others.

dangers: We did not know, and now we do: heavy use is linked to anxiety, sadness and poor sleep in teens, especially girls.
Apps are designed by experts to be hard to put down.
Strangers, predators and scams reach children here.

experts.say: Pediatricians are asking for bigger changes beyond screen-time limits. They want apps built with children's growth in mind, not just to keep them hooked, and more money for libraries, safe places to play and good non-profit media for children.
experts.who: American Academy of Pediatrics
experts.source: Contemporary Pediatrics, 'AAP calls for system-level changes to improve children's digital media environments'

experts.say: How a child uses social media can make a big difference in whether it hurts their mental health. The focus is shifting from counting minutes to caring for a child's whole well-being.
experts.who: Dr. Jenny Radesky, Co-Medical Director, AAP Center of Excellence on Social Media and Youth Mental Health
experts.source: American Academy of Pediatrics Center of Excellence on Social Media and Youth Mental Health

experts.say: A year after Australia's under-16 ban, the results are mixed. Fewer children have accounts, but many tech-savvy teens get around the rules, and a ban does not fix addictive designs or harmful feeds.
experts.who: Analysis drawing on Australia's eSafety Commissioner data
experts.source: Upstox News, 'Why social media bans can't outsmart digitally fluent teenagers'

Ten years later, in 2024, Elder Bednar repeated that call. He encouraged members to keep using social media to share the light of the gospel of Jesus Christ and help gather Israel, and to use it wisely (Deseret News: https://www.deseret.com/faith/2024/08/20/da

The Church uses its own youth social media channels, now called 'For the Strength of Youth.' Through them, young people and families around the world read and talk about the gospel together, helping the rising generation become lifelong disciples (Church Newsr

learned.note: The U.S. Surgeon General warned in 2023 that social media is not proven safe for children and teens, and several countries have since set minimum ages of 15 or 16. Waiting until at least 16 for a child's own account is now the mainstream advice.
learned.source: Surgeon General advisory, 2023; national age laws, summarised

learned.note: Teen anxiety and depression rose sharply after 2012, the year smartphones and social media reached most teenagers. Many researchers now see that as cause, not coincidence.
Studies indicate that passive engagement with short-form digital media, such as scrolling through social media feeds, is associated with higher levels of anxiety and depression among adolescents.
Research indicates that excessive use of social media platforms can negatively impact adolescents' mental health, contributing to increased anxiety and depression.
learned.source: Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development

learned.note: A global study found that high screen time, including social media use, is linked to lower academic achievement and increased mental health issues in children.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services released an advisory highlighting the risks of excessive screen use among children, linking it to increased anxiety, depression, and developmental challenges.

The National Conference of State Legislatures reported that states are implementing policies to address the mental health impacts of social media and emerging technologies on youth, including AI safeguards and digital literacy efforts.
The American Academy of Pediatrics emphasized that screen time limits alone are insufficient, advocating for a comprehensive approach to digital media use that considers content quality and context.

In the UK, the Wellcome Trust gave £9.3 million to ten research teams. They will study how new limits on social media for young people affect the wellbeing of more than 300,000 children and teens. That means families will soon have much better answers, not just guesses, about what really helps.
learned.source: CASRAI, reporting on the Wellcome Trust announcement (November 18, 2026)

learned.note: Australia doesn't let children under 16 use social media. In court, the government defended the ban by saying social media can bring children worry, sadness and worse. The government also admitted that many children still find ways around the age checks.

Instagram is now using AI around the world to spot teens who may have entered a grown-up birthday, so it can put them in safer Teen Accounts. Meta did not share how often the AI guesses age correctly, so parents should still check their children's settings themselves.
Pinterest added a new parental control that lets parents choose how much AI-made content shows up in their teen's feed. It is one of the first big social apps to give families this choice.

Boys & Girls Clubs of America says half of teens now spend four hours a day on social media. That time can push out time with friends and family in person. Talking it over helps: after one of the Clubs' programs for teen girls, 61% of them cut their social media to less than two hours a day.

Google, Meta and TikTok went to court to stop a new California law. The law would stop apps from using features like autoplay and personalized suggestions for children under 16, and it is due to start on January 1, 2027. Families will want to see what the courts decide.

studies.source: HealthyChildren.org (American Academy of Pediatrics), 'A Child-Friendly Digital World: AAP Releases New Media Recommenda
studies.finding: In its newest guidance, the American Academy of Pediatrics moved away from one fixed 'hours per day' rule for children over five. It asks families to make a Family Media Plan, to set an example with their own media habits, and to think through the '5 Cs' of media use: the Child, the Content, Calm, Crowding out other things, and Communication.

studies.source: American Academy of Pediatrics, 'Understanding the New AAP Digital Media Guidelines'
studies.finding: The AAP's Center of Excellence suggests that young people pick set times to check social media, like at lunch or after dinner, instead of letting it fill every quiet or bored moment. It also suggests other restful things to do, like music, reading or coloring.

studies.source: Engadget, reporting on Australia's eSafety Commissioner evaluation
studies.finding: Australia banned social media for children under 16 starting December 10, 2025. In early results from a two-year government study following more than 4,100 children and families, the share of under-16s with an account on a banned app fell only from 52.4% to 42.1%. Laws help a little, but what happens at home still matters most. This research is early, and the full study is not finished.

milestones.t: Instagram uses AI to spot teens worldwide
milestones.de: Meta said it is now using AI around the world to guess when someone on Instagram is a teen, even if they typed a false birthday, and then give them safer teen settings. Parents in the United States will also start seeing a short video in their feeds that explains how it works.

milestones.t: Türkiye's social media rules for children start
milestones.de: A new law in Türkiye took effect with rules for social media companies about users under 15. It is one of a growing number of countries setting age limits for social media.

bad: Looking at it instead of at the people you love.
Endless scrolling that eats evenings.
Taking it to bed.
items.why: The scriptures, the family's photos, a prophet's voice and a way to call for help, all in a pocket. This app lives here. Used with care, it is the most useful tool a family has ever carried.

ages.0-2: A parent's phone, held by the parent, for family video calls; not a toy, not a babysitter.
ages.16+: Their own phone under their own rules, learned while they were home.
ages.3-5: A parent's phone, held by the parent, for family video calls; not a toy, not a babysitter.
ages.6-9: No smartphone.
ages.10-12: No smartphone; a basic phone or a watch if the family needs one.
ages.13-15: Only with a written family agreement, filters, parent-known passwords and no bedroom overnight; many experts say wait until high school.

good: Scriptures and this app anywhere you go.
A camera for every family memory.
Maps, help and family one tap away.
harm: Every other technology on this list in one pocket, always on, always pulling.
A camera, a chat and a browser with a child at bedtime, alone.
Attention broken into pieces; the mind never rests.
kids: It sleeps in the kitchen, not in your room.
People in the room come first.
Use it to make something or reach someone, then put it down.
items.name: The Smartphone
items.talk: Let's each say one thing our phone helps with and one thing it steals.
items.what: A phone, a camera, a computer and the whole internet in one pocket. The iPhone came first; now almost everyone has one.
work: It carries the Bible and other scriptures in many languages, so God's word can be read or heard almost anywhere, by people who might never hold a printed copy.
It helps families stay close across distance, with video calls to grandparents, messages to missionaries, and family prayer together even when someone is far away.
It helps churches and neighbors serve: organizing meals for the sick, rides for the elderly, help for the poor, and quick check-ins on someone who is lonely.
It can open a window to help for the sick and struggling, such as talking with a doctor from far away, finding a crisis line, or reaching out to a friend who needs a kind word.
avoid: A smartphone in a bedroom overnight; it charges in the kitchen.
Apps installed without a parent's approval.
Deleted histories and hidden folders.
The phone at meals, in worship, and while driving.
bless: Scriptures, hymns and talks in a pocket everywhere.
Navigation to someone who needs help; a call to someone alone.
Record the stories of the old and the first words of the young.
future: Guarding your own attention: turning off notifications, putting the phone away to do deep work, and choosing when to be reachable.
Staying safe and wise online: strong passwords, protecting your privacy, spotting scams, and knowing what not to share.
Judging what is true: checking sources before believing or sharing something, especially as fake photos and AI-made content spread.
Using the phone as a tool for work and life: kind, clear messages, video calls, maps, banking, calendars and working with a team.

stages.0-2: Babies and toddlers should not have a smartphone. They learn by touching, moving and seeing loving faces, so the World Health Organization advises no screen time for babies under 1, and pediatricians note that babies do not learn from screens. A short video call with Grandma while you hold them is a gentle exception.
stages.18+: Young adults now set their own limits, and the phone is an everyday tool for school, work, money and church. Habits like phone-free meals, a set bedtime for the phone and turning off notifications that break up their focus help them stay in charge of the phone instead of the phone being in charge of them.
stages.3-5: Young children should not have a phone of their own. If they use yours, keep it under an hour a day, sit with them, and choose slow, good-quality shows so there is plenty of time left for play, sleep and stories.
stages.6-8: Children this age are still learning to stop themselves, so they should not have their own smartphone or social media. A shared family tablet or phone, used in common rooms with a parent close by, lets them learn safely while play, reading and outdoor time come first.
stages.9-11: Many friends will start getting phones now, but large studies link owning a smartphone before about 12 to worse sleep, more depression and more weight gain. Waiting is wise. If a child needs to reach you, try a simple phone that only calls and texts, and keep all devices out of bedrooms at night.
stages.12-14: Pediatricians say there is no single right age for a first smartphone. Look for signs of readiness: being honest with parents, handling arguments with friends kindly, and knowing how to tell what is true online. Start with parental controls, no social media before 13, a written family media plan and phones charging outside the bedroom at night.
stages.15-17: Teens can carry more of the load themselves as they show they can manage their time and stay safe. Keep talking every week about what they see online, protect sleep with a phone-free bedtime, and help them notice when the phone crowds out friends, schoolwork or prayer.

dangers: The average person checks it well over a hundred times a day; children learn that from us.
A phone in the bedroom steals about an hour of sleep a night.
It can put every danger of the internet into a child's hand, unwatched.

experts.say: Children who got a smartphone between ages 12 and 13 had more mental health problems and worse sleep than children who waited. Dr. Barzilay says the findings are not meant to blame parents, and his own two older children got phones before 12.
experts.who: Dr. Ran Barzilay, child and adolescent psychiatrist, Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, lead author of the Pediatrics

experts.say: Banning phones at school is not enough on its own. Overall phone and social media use is what is linked to poorer outcomes, so families and communities need wider plans as well.
experts.who: Dr. Victoria Goodyear, Associate Professor, University of Birmingham
experts.source: Phys.org report on the Lancet Regional Health – Europe study

experts.say: Social media, which most children reach through a smartphone, has some benefits. But it carries a 'profound risk of harm' to young people's mental health, so parents, tech companies and lawmakers should work together to make it safer.
experts.who: Dr. Vivek Murthy, then U.S. Surgeon General
experts.source: AAP News, on the Surgeon General's advisory

experts.say: Researchers who favor phone-free schools argue that the Lancet study's design cannot show that phone restrictions do not help. This is a reminder that experts still disagree and the research is still growing.
experts.who: After Babel, the research newsletter of social psychologist Jonathan Haidt

ldsWork: Family history in your pocket: the FamilySearch apps let children and parents add memories and photos, find ancestors, and get family names ready to take to the temple. Church leaders have taught that this work helps gather Israel on both sides of the veil.
Gospel study anywhere: the Gospel Library app puts the scriptures, general conference talks and Come, Follow Me in many languages into a family's hands every day.

Sharing light: in his 2014 talk 'To Sweep the Earth as with a Flood,' Elder David A. Bednar invited members to use technology and social media to share the message of the Restoration in good, true and uplifting ways, as part of preparing the world for the Savi

learned.note: Schools that lock phones away during the day report more talking, more play and better learning. Many countries and states now require it.
Waiting to give a child their own smartphone until high school, and a 'dumb' phone before that, is now common advice from pediatricians.

A review in Frontiers in Psychology found that excessive smartphone use among adolescents is linked to sleep disruption, reduced attention, and increased anxiety, suggesting the need for balanced usage.

A US study in the Journal of Adolescent Health found that teens who spent more time on their phones late at night, especially on social media, fell asleep later and slept less. Teens who used social media at night also said their sleep was worse. Leaving the phone outside the bedroom at night is a simple way to protect sleep.
learned.source: Medscape, reporting on a study in the Journal of Adolescent Health

studies.source: Barzilay et al., 'Smartphone Ownership, Age of Smartphone Acquisition, and Health Outcomes in Early Adolescence,' Pediat
studies.finding: In a study of 10,588 U.S. children, those who owned a smartphone at age 12 had higher odds of depression, obesity and too little sleep than those who did not. The earlier a child got a phone, the higher the risk of obesity and poor sleep. This study shows a link, not proof that phones caused the problems.

studies.source: American Academy of Pediatrics, 'Digital Ecosystems, Children, and Adolescents' policy statement, Pediatrics 157(2)
studies.finding: The American Academy of Pediatrics says research does not point to one right age for a first phone. It suggests judging readiness by the child's honesty, media skills and ability to handle conflict with others. It also recommends a family media plan, parental controls, a shared family tablet for younger children, and screen-free times for sleep, play, reading and family.

studies.source: Goodyear et al., SMART Schools study, The Lancet Regional Health – Europe
studies.finding: A study of 1,227 students in 30 English schools found that school phone bans slightly cut phone use during the school day but did not change students' overall use, mental health or grades. More time on phones overall was still linked to worse sleep, wellbeing and schoolwork. The authors say what happens at home matters too, but other researchers have questioned the study's design, so the evidence

studies.source: World Health Organization guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep for children under 5 (reported
studies.finding: The WHO recommends no screen time for babies under 1 and no more than one hour a day for children aged 2 to 4, with more active play and good sleep instead.

studies.source: Pew Research Center, 'Teens, Social Media and Mental Health'
studies.finding: In a 2025 survey, 45% of U.S. teens said they spend too much time on social media, and 44% said they had cut back on their phone and social media use. Many teens see the pull of the phone themselves and want help with it.

milestones.t: First nationwide study of school phone bans
milestones.de: Researchers from Harvard, Dartmouth and NWEA looked at students in about 4,600 U.S. schools and found that students learned a little more after phones were kept out of school. Schools that locked phones in pouches gained about 1 to 2 extra weeks of learning each year.
milestones.source: Harvard Center for Education Policy Research

bad: Autoplay that turns one video into three hours.
Videos made to shock, scare or sell.
Copying dangerous stunts.
items.why: A gospel talk, a hymn, a how-to for fixing the sink, a lesson from the best teacher in the world: streaming put good teaching within reach of every child. The Travelers' own videos will live here.

ages.16+: Decide what deserves their evenings.
ages.3-5: One short show a day, chosen by you, with you.
ages.6-9: A locked child profile, autoplay off, a daily limit.
ages.10-12: Titles chosen together; teach ratings and why.
ages.13-15: Their choices within the family's standard; talk about what they watch.

good: Learning any skill by watching someone kind explain it.
Watching a talk or a hymn together.
Stories and lessons for children, chosen by parents.
harm: Autoplay never stops; one episode becomes a night.
'Kids' profiles can still surface content no child should see.
Binge watching replaces sleep, play and people.
kids: Autoplay off. You choose the next one, with a grown-up.
Two videos, then done.
If a video is scary or weird, close it and tell someone.
items.name: Streaming Video
items.talk: What have you learned from a video that you could teach us?
items.what: Any video, any time, on any screen. YouTube, then Netflix and the rest. The next one starts by itself.
work: Sermons, hymns, Bible stories and testimonies can reach people in their own language, in places no missionary or church building has reached yet.
People who are sick, homebound or far away can still join worship services and devotionals by watching them live.
Families can watch good, uplifting videos together, such as Bible stories, and talk about them, turning screen time into time together that teaches faith.
Free video lessons on health, farming, first aid and job skills can help serve the poor and lift people in need.
avoid: Autoplay left on.
Unrated or mature titles, and a child's profile without a parental lock.
Watching alone in a bedroom.
bless: Uplifting films and talks watched together and talked over.
A family series, one episode a week, with popcorn and a rule.
Turn it off and act the story out instead.
future: Choosing on purpose: deciding what to watch and when to stop, and turning off autoplay instead of letting an app decide.
Learning from video: using online lessons and talks to learn new skills for school, work and everyday life.
Judging what is true and good: spotting ads, low-quality content and false claims in videos, and finding trustworthy sources.
Making and sharing good video: recording and editing clear, kind videos to teach, serve, or share the good news with others.

stages.0-2: Babies and toddlers learn words, feelings and trust from real faces, voices and play, so keep streaming video out of their day. Video chats with grandparents are fine. If a two-year-old watches at all, keep it short, pick slow and gentle shows, and watch together. Don't leave the TV playing in the background.
stages.18+: Young adults choose for themselves. Encourage them to watch on purpose, not by default: turn off autoplay, guard their sleep, and keep Sabbath and people ahead of screens. Watching good things with others can be a real joy.
stages.3-5: Keep watching to less than one hour a day. Choose calm, good shows before you press play, and watch with your child. Turn off autoplay so one show ends with a 'the end', because young children can't yet stop themselves. Their growing minds need play, books and people far more than screens.
stages.6-8: Pick shows together, watch in shared rooms of the home, and set a firm stopping point before you start, like 'two episodes, then outside.' Keep autoplay off and use a kids' profile. Kids' profiles still miss things, so stay nearby and talk about what your child sees.
stages.9-11: This is a good age for your child to start choosing shows, with you checking in often. Keep a set time limit, keep autoplay off, and stop screens an hour before bed. Help your child notice how apps are built to say 'one more,' so they learn to say 'not now' for themselves.
stages.12-14: Young teens are building self-control, but the part of the brain that stops 'one more video' is still growing. Keep phones, tablets and TVs out of bedrooms at night and set family screen-free times. Keep talking openly about what they watch and how it makes them feel.
stages.15-17: Give your teen more freedom, and ask them to make their own viewing plan that protects sleep, school, faith and friends. Binge-watching late at night is the main risk to watch for. Stay close and keep talking about what they watch, without spying.

dangers: Recommendation feeds can lead a child from cartoons to something harmful in a few clicks.
Some 'kids' videos are made by machines to catch attention, not to teach.

experts.say: Because of how they make money, video and media platforms are often built to keep children watching as long as possible, not to do what is best for them. So parental controls, time limits and a close parent-child relationship matter.
experts.who: American Academy of Pediatrics, Council on Communications and Media

experts.say: Research in South Korea linked children's videos showing 'negative interactions' (characters treating each other badly) to more anxiety in children. The researchers say more study is needed, and they did not find every effect they looked for.
experts.who: Researchers studying children's YouTube content in South Korea

experts.say: Media can have a good place in family life when parents think about the 5 Cs: the Child, the Content, whether media is used to Calm, whether it Crowds out other activities, and open Communication. The focus is on what children watch and why, not just how long.
experts.who: American Academy of Pediatrics
experts.source: AAP, The 5 Cs of Media Use

experts.say: Researchers studying young teens and YouTube are looking at both sides: some kids use it to calm hard feelings, but it can also cost them sleep. They found many families watch YouTube together. Researchers say knowing why children watch matters as much as counting the minutes.
experts.who: Researchers in Behavioral Sciences (peer-reviewed qualitative study)

ldsWork: General conference and other messages from living prophets and apostles are streamed and offered in many languages, so people around the world can hear the Lord's servants for themselves.
FamilySearch shares free video lessons and online events, such as RootsTech, that teach families how to find their ancestors and prepare names for temple work.

Church leaders have encouraged members to use technology wisely to share the restored gospel and help gather scattered Israel on both sides of the veil. Uplifting videos can be part of that work, especially when families also guard their time and their homes.

learned.note: Turning off autoplay and choosing videos together removes most of the harm and keeps most of the good. Watching beside a child turns a screen into a conversation.

A study in npj Digital Medicine indicated that digital mental health interventions can offer small but significant benefits for children's emotional and behavioral outcomes, especially when combined with in-person support.
The American Psychological Association emphasized that engagement with educational technology does not always equate to learning, urging careful evaluation of digital tools used in education.

studies.finding: The American Academy of Pediatrics says video platforms often use autoplay and endless scrolling that can make it harder for children to stop. It advises families to set time boundaries: less than about one hour a day for toddlers and preschoolers, and around one to two hours a day of entertainment media for school-age children and teens. Families should keep screen-free time for sleep, play, read
