studies.finding: The World Health Organization advises no screen time for babies under 1. For ages 2 to 4, it advises no more than one hour of sitting screen time a day, and says less is better, so young children can sit less, play more and sleep well.

studies.source: YouTube Viewing and Content Quality in Toddlers (peer-reviewed study, PubMed Central)
studies.finding: A study of toddlers who watched YouTube found that much of what they watched was low quality. The researchers note that watching on the main YouTube site, instead of YouTube Kids, exposes young children to unsuitable content. Many parents in the study did not know YouTube Kids existed. Choosing shows ahead of time and using kids' settings helps, but those settings are not perfect.

studies.source: Binge-watching and gender-specific effects on academic, social, and mental well-being in children and adolescents (PLOS
studies.finding: A study of children and teens in Hong Kong found binge-watching was common. It was linked to poorer sleep in boys and to other problems. The study only shows a link, not that binge-watching causes these problems, and the authors say research on children is still limited.

bad: Handing it over to keep a child quiet, for hours.
Apps full of ads and in-app buying aimed at small children.
items.why: A scripture story with pictures, a lullaby, a video call with Grandma: a tablet can bring all of it to a small child at bedtime. It was made to be simple enough for anyone to hold light and truth.

ages.0-2: None, except a video call in a parent's hands.
ages.16+: Whatever it is for, on purpose.
ages.3-5: Short spells of good apps beside a parent; about an hour of screens in all.
ages.6-9: A child account with limits; creation over consumption.
ages.10-12: Schoolwork and creating, in family rooms.
ages.13-15: A tool, with the same rules as the phone.

good: Reading illustrated scripture stories together.
Video calls with family far away.
Drawing, music and learning games chosen by parents.
harm: The easiest screen to hand a child, and so the easiest to overuse.
A quiet child on a tablet is not always a learning child.
kids: Tablet time is together time.
Ask before you tap anything that costs money.
It stays out of the bedroom.
items.name: Tablets
items.talk: What is your favourite thing we do on the tablet together? What is your favourite thing we do with no screen at all?
items.what: A big touch screen with no keyboard. Easy enough for a toddler to use, which is the point and the problem.
work: One tablet can hold the Bible in thousands of languages, in text and often in audio, so people can read and hear God's word in their own tongue (https://www.wycliffe.org/digital-bible-resources).
Families can read scriptures, sing hymns and pray together using a shared tablet, even when they live far apart, through video calls with grandparents, missionaries and loved ones.
A tablet can help people who serve the sick, the poor and the lonely to keep in touch, plan visits and share stories of hope and comfort.
Used together, a family tablet can bring parents and children closer through stories, pictures and shared learning, so they aren't each alone with a screen.
avoid: Tablet at meals, in the car for short trips, and at bedtime.
A tablet as a way to stop crying or fill every wait.
Apps with ads and in-app purchases.
bless: Read the scriptures and the stories together on it.
Draw a picture for someone and send it.
Video-call a grandparent and show them the drawing.
future: Using a touch screen to make things, like writing, drawing, recording and organizing, and not only to watch.
Choosing good apps and good information, and knowing which ones really help and which only grab your attention.
Self-control with devices: putting the tablet down when it's time, and calming down without a screen.
Using a tablet to learn, work and keep in touch with family, church and coworkers from anywhere.

stages.0-2: For babies under about 18 months, the American Academy of Pediatrics still says to avoid screen media, so keep the tablet away and use your lap, your voice and real toys. Babies learn words and feelings from faces, and a screen can't answer back the way you do.
stages.18+: Young adults choose for themselves. A tablet can be a good tool for study, work, scripture reading and family history. Habits like Sabbath rest from screens and putting devices away at meals and with people can help them stay in charge of the tool.
stages.3-5: Use the tablet a little, and best of all together, with a few good learning apps for letters and numbers. Don't use it to calm big feelings. Little children are just learning how to handle being upset, and they learn that best with your help, not a screen's.
stages.6-8: A shared family tablet in a room where everyone is, with apps and times you choose together, works better than giving the child one of their own. Children this age are building reading, friendships and play outside, so make sure the tablet doesn't crowd those out.
stages.9-11: Let the tablet help with schoolwork, making things and family history, and keep simple rules about where and when it gets used, with no tablets in bedrooms at night. Children this age can start helping write the family's media plan, which teaches them to make good choices for themselves.
stages.12-14: Before a young teen gets their own tablet, set clear limits on apps, chatting and night-time use, and check in often with kind, open talks. Young teens want to belong and are easily pulled in by what's on the screen, so they still need a parent nearby to guide them.
stages.15-17: Give teens more freedom step by step as they show they can use the tablet well for school, creating and serving others, and keep talking about sleep, friends and what they see. These years are practice for running their own lives, so the goal is good judgment, not just following rules.

dangers: Under two, screens teach almost nothing and take time from what does: faces, voices, play.
Small children cannot tell an ad from a game.

experts.say: If a child is always handed a tablet when upset, they may miss the chance to have their feelings noticed and to learn, with a parent's help, how to work through big feelings.
experts.who: Jennifer Cross, MD, pediatric behavior and development expert at NewYork-Presbyterian

experts.say: Because tablet use can feed a cycle of trouble handling feelings, the researchers think parents should wait before introducing young children to screens.
experts.who: Caroline Garon-Carrier, lead researcher on the JAMA Pediatrics tablet study

experts.say: The main lesson for families is not just how to limit screen time, but how to use screens well together as a family.
experts.who: Milkovich, speaking to EdSurge about the new AAP guidance

experts.say: Research on children and screens has become more detailed, and advice is moving away from treating every screen the same. The question now is what each child needs and what screens might be crowding out.
experts.who: The authors writing about the AAP's 2026 policy

ldsWork: President Howard W. Hunter taught in 1994 that the Church had 'begun using information technology to hasten the sacred work of providing ordinances for the deceased.' Elder Quentin L. Cook added in 2014 that family history centers are 'now in our homes,' so a

President Gordon B. Hinckley taught that the Lord inspired people to develop new technologies to move this sacred work forward. Children can use a tablet with their parents to find ancestors and hear their stories (https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/gen

President Russell M. Nelson taught that 'the Lord is hastening His work to gather Israel.' Family history, temple work and missionary work are partners in that gathering, and a tablet can help with all three (https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/liahona/2

learned.note: Pediatric guidance: no screens for children under two except video calls, and about an hour a day of good content, watched together, for young children. A tablet at bedtime delays sleep.
Experts recommend keeping tablets out of children's bedrooms overnight to prevent sleep disturbances and promote better sleep hygiene.
The APA warns that engagement with educational technology, such as tablets, does not necessarily equate to learning, urging scrutiny of EdTech claims.

Scientists in Finland followed children for eight years. They were surprised to find that kids who spent more time with screens tended to think and process information a little better as teenagers. This study shows a link, but it doesn't prove that screens caused it. So it is a gentle reminder that what we do with a screen can matter as much as how long we use it.

studies.source: The Conversation, reporting on the American Academy of Pediatrics' 2026 policy statement
studies.finding: In January 2026 the American Academy of Pediatrics dropped its old hour limits on screen time. It now asks parents to look at what screens are pushing out of a child's day. It still says to avoid screen media for children under 18 months, and for ages 2 to 5 it favors high-quality media built to teach math and reading.

studies.source: EdSurge, on the new AAP recommendations
studies.finding: The 2026 AAP guidance suggests a shared family tablet instead of giving a child their own. It also suggests offering other activities in place of screen time, finding other ways to help children calm down, and making a family media plan together.

studies.source: HealthDay News, on a study in JAMA Pediatrics
studies.finding: A Canadian study in JAMA Pediatrics found that more tablet use at age 3½ was linked to more anger and frustration by age 4½. Children who got frustrated more easily then used tablets more later, which looks like a cycle. This kind of study shows a link but can't fully prove the tablet caused it.

studies.source: Jimmy Kim and Josh Gilbert, writing about their meta-analysis
studies.finding: A Harvard-led review of 36 studies found that, on average, math and reading apps helped children ages 3 to 9 learn. But results ranged from slightly harmful to very helpful depending on the app, so which app you pick matters a lot. This review is a few years old.

studies.source: The Bump, on Common Sense Media's 2025 Census on Media Use by Kids Ages 0-8
studies.finding: Common Sense Media's 2025 survey found that 40% of children have their own tablet by age 2 and 60% by age 4, even though most parents say they are worried about screens.

bad: Ordering people around instead of asking politely.
Letting it replace looking things up and thinking.
items.why: 'Play the Lantern Lullaby.' 'Read tonight's story.' A voice assistant can put scripture and music in a room with no screen at all, and help a grandparent who cannot see the buttons.

ages.16+: Use it to free time for what matters.
ages.3-5: Ask it to play a song, with 'please', beside you.
ages.6-9: Timers, music and simple questions; teach that it can be wrong.
ages.10-12: A tool, not an oracle; check what it says.
ages.13-15: Learn what it records and who hears it.

good: Playing hymns and stories with no screen.
Helping someone who cannot see or type.
Timers, reminders and answers for a busy family.
harm: A microphone that is always listening in the home.
A child who orders a 'person' around learns to order people around.
It answers with confidence whether it is right or wrong.
kids: Say please, even to the speaker.
Ask a grown-up before you ask it something big.
It is not a friend; it is a tool.
items.name: Voice Assistants
items.talk: If our speaker could only do one thing for our family, what should it be?
items.what: A speaker you talk to. Alexa, Siri and Google answer questions, play music and set timers.
work: Families can listen to the scriptures and hymns aloud at home, while cooking, driving or getting ready for bed, so God's word fills the day
Voice tools help people who cannot see well, cannot read yet, or cannot use their hands easily to hear the word and stay connected
Reminders and timers can help families keep regular times for prayer, scripture study and serving others
Children with speech difficulties may practice speaking with patient, judgment-free help, which blesses those who struggle
avoid: Purchases left enabled.
A speaker in a child's bedroom.
Asking it questions of right and wrong that belong to parents and to prayer.
bless: Play a hymn or a scripture story while hands are busy.
Timers for chores and for screens.
A voice for someone who cannot see or type.
future: Giving clear, precise spoken instructions to voice and AI tools to get work done
Checking a machine's confident answer against trusted sources before acting on it
Managing privacy settings and knowing what is recorded, stored and shared
Using voice tools to organize time, reminders and tasks while staying in charge of their own attention

stages.0-2: Babies and toddlers learn words from real faces and voices, so a talking speaker should not stand in for a parent. If one plays music or a lullaby while you hold and sing to your child, that is fine.
stages.18+: Young adults choose for themselves. Encourage them to use these tools on purpose to serve, learn and work well, to protect their privacy, and to keep real people at the center of their lives.
stages.3-5: Young children often think the speaker is a kind of person and can grow attached to it. Use it together for songs, stories and timers, and gently explain that it is a machine. Keep it in a shared room, not in the child's bedroom.
stages.6-8: Children this age believe confident answers easily. Let them ask it questions with you nearby, and check some of the answers together in a book or with a grown-up. Teach them to speak kindly, because the habits they practice on a machine are the habits they practice in their hearts.
stages.9-11: Older children can use it for homework facts, spelling and reminders. Teach them that it can be wrong, that an honest "I don't know" is a good answer, and that the microphone can save what they say.
stages.12-14: Young teens can learn to manage the privacy settings themselves, such as reviewing and deleting recordings. As newer assistants become chatty AI, talk openly about not turning to a machine for comfort or secrets that belong with family and trusted people.
stages.15-17: Teens can use voice tools to plan their time, study and build skills they will need at work. Keep talking with them about where their words and data go and about checking facts before they trust them.

dangers: It is always listening for its name; treat it as a microphone in the room.
Children can ask it anything, and it will answer.

experts.say: Amazon agreed to pay $25 million to settle U.S. government claims that Alexa kept children's voice recordings and location data, and sometimes ignored parents' requests to delete them. Parents should check and delete stored recordings.
experts.who: U.S. Federal Trade Commission and Department of Justice

experts.say: As talking AI spreads, many teens turn to chatbots for friendship and emotional support. Experts recommend that parents make it normal to talk about this, because children may be shy to admit it.
experts.who: American Psychological Association

experts.say: People, and especially children who are still learning how to talk with others, often treat voice assistants like social beings. Researchers worry that talking to them harshly again and again could shape communication habits, and they are studying this over years.
experts.who: Researchers publishing in Behaviour & Information Technology
experts.source: 'Alexa, shut up!' A 2.5-year study of communication with voice assistants in the family home

experts.say: Children ages 5 to 7 often gave smart speakers human-like qualities and formed emotional attachments to them, while parents saw them as tools. Families need to talk about what these devices really are.
experts.who: Researchers in a long-term study of parents and children using smart speakers
experts.source: "He Is Just Like Me": A Study of the Long-Term Use of Smart Speakers by Parents and Children

ldsWork: The Church offers Gospel Voice, an official skill for Alexa and Google Assistant speakers. Families can listen to the scriptures, Come, Follow Me, general conference and Church music at home, which supports home-centered gospel learning.

The Church introduced Gospel Voice as part of its "Hear Him" emphasis. Families can use it to fill their homes with the words of prophets and the scriptures, so children can learn to hear the Savior's voice.

learned.note: Children who say 'please' and 'thank you' to a speaker keep saying it to people. Manners with machines are practice for manners with everyone.

studies.source: Is it OK if Alexa doesn't know? Children and adults' beliefs about smart speaker virtuous ignorance (Proceedings of the
studies.finding: Children are not easily fooled by a confident machine as they grow. As they get older, children (like adults) increasingly judge a smart speaker that honestly says it cannot know something as more trustworthy than one that gives an exact answer to an unknowable question. Teaching children to value honest answers matters.

studies.source: Children's Trust in and Learning From Voice Assistants (peer-reviewed study)
studies.finding: Children ages 6 to 10 did not simply treat voice assistants as people. How much they trusted and learned from the device changed with age, so grown-up guidance should fit the child's age.

studies.source: Digital Wellness Lab, Key Takeaways from Our 2024 Pulse Survey on Voice Assistants & GenAI; Behaviour & Information Tech
studies.finding: In a 2024 survey by Boston Children's Hospital's Digital Wellness Lab, most parents said their children often or always say "please" and "thank you" to voice assistants. Researchers who followed families for two and a half years are still studying whether rude talk to a device carries over to how children treat people. The research is early.

studies.source: Smart speakers are an acceptable and feasible speech practice tool for children with speech difficulties (Disability and
studies.finding: A small study found smart speakers were an acceptable and workable speech-practice tool for children with speech difficulties. It may help through spaced practice, quick feedback and less fear of being judged. The evidence is still early.

bad: Disappearing into a fake world instead of living in the real one.
Games and rooms where strangers get close to children.
items.why: Walk through Jerusalem as it was. Stand in a temple far away. See the earth from space. Made well, it lets a family stand where the scriptures happened.

ages.16+: A tool for learning and creating, with their own limits.
ages.3-5: None.
ages.6-9: None.
ages.10-12: Only what the maker allows, in the family room, short sessions, no social VR.
ages.13-15: Short sessions, no strangers, parents can see what is played.

good: Visiting holy places and history together.
Training doctors and pilots without risk.
Helping people who cannot travel see the world.
harm: Young eyes and balance are still developing; makers set minimum ages for a reason.
A headset shuts out the room and the family.
Social VR puts strangers, and their voices and hands, right beside a child.
kids: Only with a grown-up in the room.
Short turns, then take it off.
Never meet anyone in there you do not know in real life.
items.name: Virtual Reality
items.talk: If you could stand in one scripture story for five minutes, which one would it be?
items.what: A headset that covers your eyes and puts you inside a picture. You look around and it looks back.
work: Serving the sick: hospitals use VR to teach children how to stay safe while they are patients, a small way to care for those who are hurting.
Protecting children: VR lessons can let children practice water safety, earthquake safety and staying safe from harm in a place where mistakes don't hurt anyone.
Strengthening families: used together in the family room, for short turns, with a parent close by, VR can be something to share and talk about instead of something that shuts family out.
avoid: A headset under the maker's minimum age, and under 12 in most homes.
Social VR rooms with strangers.
Long sessions; twenty minutes is plenty.
bless: Walk the streets of Jerusalem, stand in a temple, see the place a scripture happened.
Visit the town a great-grandparent came from.
Learn a skill safely: surgery, flying, repair.
future: Learning and training in VR. Doctors, nurses, pilots, builders and safety workers already practice hard or dangerous tasks in VR before doing them for real.
Knowing your own limits: noticing tired eyes, dizziness or lost time, then taking off the headset and coming back to the real room.
Staying safe and kind in shared virtual spaces: using privacy, block and report tools, protecting personal information, and treating people there as real people.
Telling real from made: understanding that a world that feels real was built by someone, and asking who made it and why.

stages.0-2: No headset at all. Babies and toddlers learn to see, reach and balance in the real world and from real faces. Headset makers don't allow children this young.
stages.18+: Young adults choose for themselves. Encourage them to use VR as a tool for learning, work and serving others, and not to let it crowd out sleep, real friends, family and worship.
stages.3-5: Not yet. Little children are still learning what is real and what is pretend, and the headset's maker does not allow use under age 10. Real blocks, books and laps are better.
stages.6-8: Wait. Popular headsets like Meta Quest are not made for children under 10. If your child is curious, let them watch you try it, or look at a 3D picture together on a flat screen.
stages.9-11: From age 10, use only a parent-managed account. Keep it to short turns in a shared family room, choose calm learning apps, and turn off chatting with strangers. One small study found no harm to eyes or balance from about an hour a day in children aged 10 to 12, but the research is still early.
stages.12-14: Still use parent supervision and short turns, with breaks to rest the eyes and body. Stay out of open social worlds where adults can talk to children. At this age, children want to belong, and strangers can take advantage of that.
stages.15-17: Teens can use VR more on their own, with family rules about time, place and privacy settings. Talk openly about who they meet in VR and what to do if someone makes them uneasy. Point them to VR that builds skills, like science, design, safety and job training.

dangers: Headsets are not recommended for young children's eyes and balance.
In a virtual room, a stranger can stand right next to your child.

experts.say: Former Meta workers say the company held back its own research about risks to children in VR. One example: a teen said his 10-year-old brother was sexually propositioned in Horizon Worlds. Meta denies the claims. Either way, parents should not count on the company alone to keep children safe in social VR.
experts.who: Former Meta VR researchers (whistleblowers); Meta's denial
experts.source: Game Developer, 'Former Meta employees allege company squashed research into VR child abuse' (September 10, 2025)

experts.say: The children's advocacy group Fairplay filed a complaint with the U.S. Federal Trade Commission. It says Meta's VR world Horizon Worlds is full of children under 13, many using adult accounts, where they can meet harassment.
experts.who: Fairplay (children's advocacy group)
experts.source: Fairplay request for investigation to the Federal Trade Commission (April 10, 2025)

experts.say: The researchers who tested 10- to 12-year-olds say moderate VR use may be fairly low-risk for children that age. They also say more study is needed.
experts.who: Karol Silva, Nichole Breeland, Ashley Clark, Ilke Öztekin and Rachel Kelly, study authors
experts.source: Exponent, 'Is Virtual Reality Safe for Children?'

experts.say: Stanford researchers who worked with Common Sense Media warned that VR is likely to affect children powerfully, because the body and mind can react to it almost as if it were real. That is why they advised short sessions. This report is older (2018), but its main caution still holds.
experts.who: Stanford University researchers with Common Sense Media
experts.source: UploadVR, 'Report Outlines Potential Risks With Use Of VR By Kids'

learned.note: Makers set minimum ages of about 10 to 13 for headsets, and reports of harassment in virtual rooms led to 'personal boundary' settings. Treat a headset like the internet with the door open.
learned.source: Manufacturer guidance and safety reports, summarised

studies.source: Silva, Breeland, Clark, Öztekin & Kelly, 'Effects of virtual reality use in children aged 10 to 12 years,' Frontiers in
studies.finding: Children aged 10 to 12 used VR for 60 minutes a day for four days in a row. Researchers found no harm to their eyesight, balance, hand-eye coordination or self-control, though a few children felt mildly sick, as with motion sickness. The study was small and short, and it was run by scientists at a consulting firm, so the research is still early.

studies.source: Liao, Kamsin & Mohd Noor, 'The efficacy and safety of immersive virtual reality in children's safety training: a systema
studies.finding: A review of many studies found that VR is a promising way to teach children safety, such as water safety, earthquake safety and preventing violence. The reviewers also looked at how safe the headsets are for children. Results are encouraging, but there are still only a few studies on each topic.

studies.source: Hyeon et al., 'Virtual reality education for preventing safety incidents in pediatric hospital settings,' Journal of Ped
studies.finding: Nurses built and tested a VR lesson that teaches children in the hospital how to avoid accidents there, such as falls. This shows VR used for a short time, with a clear purpose and an adult nearby.

studies.source: Meta, 'Meta Quest Safety Information for Parents and Pre-teens'
studies.finding: The maker of the most popular headsets says children under 10 cannot use Meta Quest 2 and 3. A parent must create and manage the account for a child aged 10 to 12. Ages may differ by country.

bad: Fake pictures, voices and videos made to lie or shame.
Cheating on schoolwork and never learning.
Chatbots pretending to be friends, or worse, to lonely people.
items.why: AI can read every book ever written and explain any of them to a child in plain words. It can help a family write its history, help a doctor find a cure, help a missionary speak a new language. Light and knowledge, faster than ever - the last great tool before the Lord comes, if it is used for Him.

ages.0-2: None; a parent may use it to help them.
ages.16+: Learn to use it well and honestly; it will be part of their work.
ages.3-5: None; a parent may use it to help them.
ages.6-9: Only with a parent beside them, in a family-safe tool.
ages.10-12: With a parent, for learning; never alone with a chatbot; check facts together.
ages.13-15: School-approved tools; never AI companions; learn to verify; honest about what is theirs.

good: Explaining anything, at any level, patiently.
Helping people who cannot see, hear or speak.
Doing hours of hard work in seconds so people can do what only people can do.
harm: It is confident when it is wrong, and a child cannot always tell.
Deepfakes: anyone's face and voice on anything, including a child's.
AI 'companions' pull lonely children from real friends and real family, and some have encouraged self-harm.
Doing the thinking for them, so they never learn to.
kids: AI can be wrong. Check it, especially about people and facts.
Never share private things or pictures with an AI.
It is a tool, not a friend. Real friends are people.
items.name: AI That Talks
items.talk: What is one thing you would love AI to help our family do? What is one thing we should never let it do?
items.what: Computers that write, draw, talk and answer like a person. ChatGPT came first; now AI is in phones, cars, schools and hospitals.
avoid: Sharing private things, pictures or family details with any AI.
AI 'friends' and companion apps at any age of childhood.
Using it to do schoolwork and calling it their own.
Chatting with it alone before they are old enough to check it.
bless: Explain a scripture at their level, patiently, as many times as they ask.
Write the family's history from grandpa's recordings.
Learn a language, a skill, a subject the school does not teach.
Help with the Lord's work: translation, teaching, reaching.
future: Checking AI's answers: knowing it can be wrong while sounding sure, and checking facts against trusted sources before believing or sharing them.
Asking clear, good questions and giving clear directions, so AI becomes a useful helper and not a crutch.
Thinking and writing for yourself first, then using AI to improve your work, while staying honest about what is yours.
Guarding your privacy and your face and voice online, and spotting fakes made by AI.

stages.0-2: Babies and toddlers should not use talking AI. They learn words, feelings and trust from real faces and voices, so their time is best spent with you, being held, talked to and played with.
stages.18+: Young adults choose for themselves, but they still do well with family values to steer by: use AI as a tool, check what it says, keep real friendships first, and stay honest about what is your own work. Keep talking with them about it as equals.
stages.3-5: Young children should not use AI chatbots on their own. They often believe a talking machine is alive or is their friend. If a parent uses AI to answer a question together, sit side by side and say plainly, "This is a computer program, not a person."
stages.6-8: If your child uses AI at this age, it should be rare and done together with you, for things like looking up a fact and then checking it in a book. Children this age are just learning to read, write and work out problems themselves, and that hard work is what grows their minds.
stages.9-11: Children this age can use AI with an adult nearby and with clear rules: no secrets, no sharing names, photos or where they live, and do your own homework first. This is a good age to teach them that AI can be wrong while sounding sure, so they learn to check what it says.
stages.12-14: Young teens can use AI for school when a teacher or parent allows it, but should stay away from AI 'companion' or 'friend' apps. A large 2025 survey found that younger teens trust AI advice more than older teens do. Keep devices in shared rooms, and talk often about what they are asking it.
stages.15-17: Older teens can use AI as a helper for brainstorming, practicing and explaining things, but not to do their thinking or their friendships for them. Help them learn to use it well and honestly, because they will need these skills at work, and ask them to come to you, not a chatbot, with big worries.

dangers: AI is confident even when it is wrong; check what it says.
A deepfake can put anyone's face on anything.
AI 'companions' can pull a child away from real friends and real family. Some have encouraged self-harm.
Nobody fully knows yet what growing up with AI does to a child. That is why this page updates.

experts.say: AI made to act like a person can blur the line between a real friend and a machine. Teens may find this harder to see than adults do, so healthy limits on these 'relationships' matter.
experts.who: American Psychological Association
experts.source: Health Advisory: Artificial Intelligence and Adolescent Well-being

experts.say: If people lean on AI to think and write for them, they may build up a kind of 'cognitive debt': the work gets done, but less learning stays with them. The researchers say more study is needed.
experts.who: Researchers at the MIT Media Lab
experts.source: Your Brain on ChatGPT (MIT Media Lab)

experts.say: There is a good side too. Teens who understand how AI works, and where it falls short, are better prepared to use it wisely and safely in school, work and life.
experts.who: American Psychological Association
experts.source: AI literacy: Why every teen needs to learn this essential skill

learned.note: Deepfake scams that copy a family member's voice are now common. Families are choosing a secret 'safe word' so a real call can be told from a fake one.

Several AI chatbots have been found giving harmful advice to teens, and lawsuits followed. Makers added age checks and parent controls. A child's AI use, like their internet use, belongs where a parent can see it.
The American Psychological Association highlighted concerns that AI tools, while offering educational benefits, may interfere with children's cognitive and social development if misused.
A recent review highlights that excessive use of generative AI by adolescents is linked to increased mental health issues, including anxiety and depression.
A study discusses the benefits and risks of AI in pediatric healthcare, emphasizing the need for ethical considerations to protect children's mental health.
Recent developments in AI-driven educational tools show promise in enhancing personalized learning experiences for children, though concerns about data privacy remain.
A UK parliamentary briefing discussed the cognitive and health impacts of screen and AI use on children, noting both benefits and risks, including potential sleep disruption and attention issues.
Research reviewed the use of digital health technologies and AI in mitigating mental health impacts of adverse childhood experiences, highlighting potential benefits and implementation challenges.

The American Psychological Association warned that while educational technology can engage students, it doesn't always lead to actual learning, especially with generative AI tools that may improve immediate performance without building underlying knowledge.

The American Academy of Pediatrics highlighted potential dangers of AI for children, including privacy erosion and exposure to biased or harmful content, urging for cautious integration of AI in children's lives.

New York passed a new law to keep children safer when they talk with AI chatbots. Starting January 1, 2027, chatbot companies may not give children in New York unsafe 'AI companion' features, and they will have to check users' ages. This is a good time to talk together about which helpers in your home can talk back.
learned.source: Holland & Knight, 'New York Enacts AI Chatbot Safeguards for Minors' (November 5, 2026)

learned.note: The American Psychological Association looked at the new toys that talk using AI. Experts worry these toys can make little children feel too attached to them. The toys also don't teach the things a real person does, like sharing and taking turns. For very young children, real people still matter most: a parent, a grandparent, a friend.
learned.source: American Psychological Association, Monitor on Psychology, 'Chatbots in the crib' (November 1, 2026)

learned.note: A big new survey of 1,211 American children aged 9 to 17 found that nearly half of 9- to 12-year-olds have already used an AI chatbot or AI companion. That is younger than the age of 13 that most of these chatbots are made for. Many children say they use AI for homework, and some use it when they feel stressed or lonely. That is a good reason for families to talk about it together.
learned.source: Common Sense Media, The 2026 Common Sense Media Census: Tech and Media Use by Tweens and Teens (reported by NPR)

learned.note: United Nations child-protection leaders warned that bad people are using AI in new ways to trick and harm children online, and that protections are not keeping up. Children are safest when they know they can always tell a trusted grown-up if something online feels wrong.

Boys & Girls Clubs of America also says more teens are turning to AI chatbots when they need someone to talk to. A chatbot can be a handy helper, but it cannot love you the way your family and friends do. When your heart feels heavy, talk to a real person first.

Ofcom, which looks after TV and the internet in the UK, found that about 8 in 10 UK children are now using AI chatbots, and some use them for company. Most parents like that chatbots help children learn and do homework. About half worry that children might let the chatbot do their thinking for them.

A study from Harvard and Boston Children's Hospital, published in JAMA Pediatrics, asked parents about using AI chatbots to help children with their feelings and mental health. About 3 in 4 parents said they were not comfortable with it. The same report says some young people already ask chatbots for this kind of help without telling their parents.

studies.source: MIT Media Lab, "Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task"
studies.finding: In a small study of 54 adults writing essays, the people who used ChatGPT showed less brain engagement than those who wrote on their own, and most of them could not correctly quote what they had just written. This is early research. It has not yet been fully peer-reviewed, and it studied adults, not children, but it suggests that letting AI do the writing can mean we learn less.

studies.source: Common Sense Media survey, reported by ScienceAlert
studies.finding: A nationally representative survey of 1,060 U.S. teens aged 13 to 17 found that 72% had used an AI companion at least once and 52% used one a few times a month. Younger teens (13 to 14) were more likely than older teens to trust advice from these systems.

studies.source: American Psychological Association, Health Advisory: Artificial Intelligence and Adolescent Well-being
studies.finding: The American Psychological Association advises that AI tools for teenagers should be built differently from those for adults. It also advises that teens need protection from AI that pretends to be a human friend, and that parents, schools and companies all share the job of keeping teens safe.

studies.source: American Psychological Association, "AI literacy: Why every teen needs to learn this essential skill"
studies.finding: The APA says that knowing how AI works, along with what it is good for, what it gets wrong and its risks, has become an essential skill for teens. It encourages teaching this 'AI literacy' at home and at school.

milestones.t: New York limits AI companions for children
milestones.de: New York signed a law that starts on January 1, 2027. It says AI chatbots must not use unsafe 'companion' features with children, such as pretending to be a human or to have real feelings. Companies will also have to check users' ages.

milestones.t: Oregon sues a chatbot maker over child safety
milestones.de: Oregon's Attorney General started a 'Keeping Kids Safe' program and sued OpenAI for about $2 billion. The state says the company's ChatGPT chatbot put children in danger and misled parents about how safe it is. The state also asked parents to talk with their children about which AI chatbots they use and what they say to them.

milestones.t: New AI models from OpenAI and Google
milestones.de: In one busy week, OpenAI released new GPT-6.2 models and Google released Gemini 4 models. Talking AI keeps changing quickly, so families may want to look at their safety settings again.

milestones.t: New York signs a law on AI chatbots and children
milestones.de: New York's governor signed a law that requires AI chatbot companies to check users' ages and limits companion features that could be unsafe for children. It is set to take effect in 2027.

milestones.t: Colorado adopts rules for AI chatbot age checks
milestones.de: Colorado adopted new rules for its AI chatbot law. Under the rules, chatbot companies cannot rely only on an ID card to check a user's age.

milestones.t: New York bans AI chatbot toys for five years
milestones.de: New York passed a five-year ban on making and selling toys that hold AI chatbot conversations with children, after tests found unsafe chats and weak controls. The ban starts in 90 days, so it will not cover this year's holiday shopping.

milestones.t: New York pauses AI chatbot toys
milestones.de: New York's governor signed a law that stops toys with built-in AI chatbots, like talking stuffed animals, dolls and robots, from being sold for five years. California recently did something similar, and Pennsylvania is thinking about it too.

Replacing people's work without caring what happens to them.
items.why: A robot can do work that is dangerous, dull or dirty so that people are free for family, service and learning. A self-driving car may one day stop the crashes that take so many families.

ages.16+: Use them to serve, and keep the human in charge.
ages.3-5: Toy robots; learn that a machine only does what it is told.
ages.6-9: A first building kit with a grown-up.
ages.10-12: Robotics club; code something that moves.
ages.13-15: Build, program, compete; learn what the machine cannot do.

good: Dangerous jobs done without anyone getting hurt.
Help for people who cannot walk, lift or see.
Cars that never text and never fall asleep.

A car that drives itself still needs a driver who is awake.
Worry about work and the future can weigh on a teenager.

Machines do jobs; people do love.
Learn to make things with your hands too.
items.name: Robots and Self-Driving Machines
items.talk: If a robot did all the chores, what would our family do with the extra hours?
items.what: Machines with AI inside that move: cars that drive themselves, robots that build, deliver, clean and help.
work: Self-driving rides and delivery robots can help older people, people with disabilities and others who cannot drive get to church, to the doctor and to the people they love.
Robots that carry heavy loads and deliver supplies can speed up help to the hungry, the sick and families hit by disaster.
When machines take on dangerous or tiring work, people have more time and strength to love their neighbors, serve and be with family.
Building and fixing robots can be a way for young people to use their God-given talents to serve others and support a family.
avoid: Standing near robots, mowers or self-driving cars at work.
Trusting an autopilot with your life or anyone else's.
Fear; a robot is a tool, and tools serve people.
bless: Robots that help the disabled walk, see and speak.
Build a robot at home or in a club; that is learning to serve with machines.
Deliver help farther and faster than hands can reach.
future: Knowing what a machine can and cannot do, so you stay alert and ready to take over instead of trusting it blindly.
Working side by side with robots by setting them up, checking their work, fixing them and keeping people safe around them.
Basic coding and problem-solving, so robots feel like tools you understand and not mysteries you fear.
The human gifts machines lack: kindness, honesty, teamwork and good judgment about what is right.

stages.0-2: Babies and toddlers should not ride in or play near robots or self-driving machines unless a grown-up is holding them or has them safely buckled in a car seat. Little ones move fast and don't understand danger yet, and a moving machine may not see or stop for someone so small.
stages.18+: Young adults can use self-driving rides and robots wisely and should learn to work alongside them in school and at work. As adults they carry the full duty to watch the road, keep others safe and use these tools to bless the people around them.
stages.3-5: Young children can watch robots and self-driving cars from a safe place with a parent, and they can learn one rule: a machine is not a friend that will always stop for them. At this age children learn safety by doing the same thing every day, like holding hands near streets and keeping away from robot mowers and vacuums while they are running.
stages.6-8: Children this age can learn how robots work by playing with simple robot kits and coding toys while a grown-up is close by. Keep teaching them to cross the street with care, because even a careful robotaxi has struck a child near a school.
stages.9-11: Older children can build and program small robots at school or at home, which grows their curiosity, patience and problem-solving. Help them see that a machine only follows the rules people give it, so they always need to look, listen and use their own judgment near cars and moving machines.
stages.12-14: Young teens can enjoy robotics clubs, and where a parent allows it they may ride a robotaxi made for teens, such as Waymo's teen accounts, which need a parent's permission. They are starting to think about their future, so talk calmly about worries over robots taking jobs, and remind them that God gives each person gifts and that new work comes along with new tools.
stages.15-17: Teens learning to drive should know that features like lane-keeping and cruise control do not drive the car by themselves, and that the driver must stay awake, watch the road and keep phones put away. Talk with them about the careers that robots open up, and help them build skills and good character so they can face the future with hope instead of fear.

dangers: A machine that moves can hurt someone if it is wrong.
When work disappears, families need a plan; that is a job for people, not machines.

experts.say: Researchers who study car safety warn that people rely too much on partial automation. For these systems to earn a good rating, they must make sure drivers are looking at the road and have their hands ready to take control if the technology makes a mistake.
experts.who: David Kidd, researcher at the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety

experts.say: The U.S. traffic safety agency is checking whether a robotaxi took enough care near an elementary school at drop-off time, given how many young walkers were nearby. The concern is that school zones need extra caution from self-driving cars.
experts.who: U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA)

experts.say: Waymo said its computer tests showed that a fully attentive human driver would have hit the child at about 14 mph, much faster than its robotaxi did. This is the hope for self-driving cars: that they react faster than people. But it is the company's own claim, and the government is still reviewing it.
experts.who: Waymo, as reported to NHTSA

Members can use the time and help that new machines give them for family history and temple service, which Church leaders have called a key part of the gathering of Israel on both sides of the veil.

learned.note: Self-driving taxis now run in several cities with fewer crashes than human drivers in those same streets, and the arguments about who is responsible when one fails are just beginning.

studies.source: Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) ratings, as reported by Repairer Driven News
studies.finding: When the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety tested 14 partial driving automation systems, only one earned an 'acceptable' rating for its safeguards. The tests showed these systems do not do enough to keep drivers watching the road and ready to take over, and IIHS notes that cars with these features are not self-driving.

studies.source: Automotive World, reporting on a U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration investigation

The U.S. traffic safety agency (NHTSA) opened an investigation into whether the car took enough care near the school and around young walkers. Dependence on technology for family management may reduce personal interaction.

Reduces the time parents spend on coordinating family activities.
Provides a centralized platform for family communication and planning.

Discuss with parents how the AI can help with family activities.
Ensure screen time is balanced with offline family interactions.
items.name: Family AI
items.talk: How do you feel about using an AI to help manage our family's daily activities?
items.what: An AI platform designed to assist families in managing daily schedules, tasks, and home routines.
dangers: Data breaches could expose sensitive family information.
Overreliance on AI may diminish traditional family communication skills.

learned.note: Nori, the world's first Family AI, was launched to assist families in managing daily schedules and tasks.

Toys with AI chatbots inside are showing up in stores fast, and child experts writing for the American Psychological Association say these toys don't help little ones learn to share or take turns the way a real person does. Experts are asking toy makers to add stronger safety checks, privacy protections and parent controls. They also don't want toys designed to make children feel too attached to them.
learned.source: American Psychological Association, Monitor on Psychology

learned.note: Groups that look out for children wrote an open letter asking big online shops to stop selling talking AI toys before the holidays. They found 28 of these toys for sale, and more than half cost less than £50. They also pointed to a test that found more than a quarter of the toys' answers were not right for children. A cuddly toy should be a friend you can trust, so ask a grown-up before you bring one home that talks back.
learned.source: Fairplay, Alliance 4 Children and Set@16 (open letter to online marketplaces)

stages.0-2: Babies and toddlers should not use Family AI. They learn by being held, talked to, and played with by real people. Parents can use it quietly in the background so they have more time to be with their little one.
stages.3-5: Young children should not use it on their own. A parent can show them a simple picture of the day's plan, made with the app, and talk it over together. At this age children learn routines best from a loving voice, not a screen.
stages.6-8: Children this age can look at a shared family chore list or calendar with a parent beside them. They should not have their own account or type in private details. They are just learning what is private, so a grown-up keeps the keys.
stages.9-11: Children this age can check off their own tasks inside a family account that a parent sets up and watches. Talk often about why we never share addresses, school names, or where we will be with anyone online. Children this age are building habits of responsibility and can learn that the app is a helper, not the boss.
stages.12-14: Young teens can start planning some of their own schedule in the family account, with parents still able to see the settings. Talk together about how the AI can be wrong, and about keeping family information safe. These years are a good time to practice planning while parents stay close.
stages.15-17: Teens can manage more of their own calendar and tasks, and can help choose the privacy settings with their parents. They should still talk face to face about plans and feelings, not just send updates through the app. They are getting ready to run their own lives, and these skills will help them later.
stages.18+: Young adults can choose and run their own planning tools. They should read the privacy terms and decide wisely what to share. They can use these helpers to make time for family, service, and worship, while keeping real conversations at the center of home life.

studies.finding: Psychologists warn that AI tools can offer some support to young people, but they can also lead to unhealthy dependence and blur the line between talking with a person and talking with a machine. AI made for teens should be built with how teens grow in mind.
studies.source: American Psychological Association, Health Advisory: Artificial Intelligence and Adolescent Well-Being

studies.finding: In a UK study, many children kept relying on AI chatbots for information even though they knew the chatbots can get things wrong. The researchers say children cannot handle these tools alone and need adults to guide them.
studies.source: Internet Matters, 'Me, myself and AI: Understanding and safeguarding children's use of AI chatbots'

studies.finding: The American Academy of Pediatrics says generative AI offers both promise and risk. It also notes that children are underrepresented in the data most AI tools learn from. Its new policy covers doctors' use of AI only. Guidance for families' own use is still being written, so research on family use is early.
studies.source: American Academy of Pediatrics policy statement, via EurekAlert!

experts.say: Understanding how AI works, what it does well, and where it falls short is now a key skill for teens. AI answers can seem neutral and correct when they are not.
experts.who: American Psychological Association expert panel (including Craig Watkins, PhD, University of Texas at Austin)
experts.source: APA, 'AI literacy: Why every teen needs to learn this essential skill'

experts.say: As AI spreads, people are more and more asked to question what they see and hear, instead of simply trusting it.
experts.who: Brendesha Tynes, PhD, University of Southern California, APA health advisory panel member

experts.say: Generative AI is already helping and improving fast. But few tools have been carefully tested with children, so developers should design them with children's needs in mind.
experts.who: American Academy of Pediatrics
experts.source: EurekAlert! news release on AAP policy statement

experts.say: Family AI tools that handle calendars, health reminders, and children's schedules hold some of a family's most sensitive information, such as where the children are after school. That makes privacy protections very important.
experts.who: Technology reporting on family AI assistants

future: Planning time and tasks with digital helpers, while still making your own choices about what matters most
Checking AI suggestions and catching mistakes instead of trusting them blindly
Guarding private information: knowing what to share, what to keep safe, and how to use privacy settings
Working with others on shared plans, while knowing when a talk face to face is better than a message
work: Setting a regular time for family prayer, scripture reading, and worship, so the busy week does not crowd them out
Organizing meals, rides, and visits for neighbors who are sick, grieving, or in need, so no one is forgotten
Handling small chores and reminders, so parents have more time to listen to, teach, and love their children
Coordinating family service projects and helping each child see where they can serve

agesNote: Children do not grow all at once. What a two-year-old needs from a screen (almost nothing) and what a sixteen-year-old needs (practice governing themselves) are different, so this guide is written by stage: Babies & Toddlers, then the same six stages the Morning Lantern uses. The stages follow how a child's mind, body and conscience develop, and lean on the American Academy of Pediatrics, the World Health Organization, the U.S. Surgeon General and the American Psychological Association, and on the counsel in For the Strength of Youth. Every line is a starting point for a family's own rules, not a substitute for them.
principle: Light and knowledge build on light and knowledge. Nothing is invented alone: every new thing stands on something that came before it, and Heavenly Father gives it so His work can go forward. The same tool can bless a family or hurt one. Knowing which is which is the whole lesson.
modernNote: The parent's guide - what it can do to a child, what to stay away from, blessing others, and what fits at each age - is written for the tools of today, from the Internet on. The older technologies are here for the story of how one light led to the next.
